about: Infection and Defence (MBBS0014) is the second of the four systems modules in UCL's MBBS Year 1, taught in person in Term 1 (in 2026–27, four weeks in November, before CIF Week A) and carrying 0 credits. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue says it introduces infectious agents and how they cause disease, the body's defences against them, the epidemiology of infection, its social and psychological consequences for patients, and how anti-infective drugs work. UCL does not publish a topic list, so the topics here follow the order of that official description. Year 1 knowledge is tested in the end-of-year integrated Applied Knowledge Tests.
topics: Bacteria: structure, identification and how they cause disease
Adaptive immunity: T cells, B cells and antibodies
Immune memory, vaccination and when defences fail
Epidemiology, transmission and control of infection
Social and psychological effects of infection on patients
How antimicrobial drugs act, resistance and stewardship

notes.h: Bacteria: structure, identification and how they cause disease
notes.overview: Bacteria are prokaryotes, and their structure explains how we identify them, how they cause disease and why antibiotics can hit them without harming us. This topic links cell wall type to the Gram stain, follows the steps from colonisation to disease, and contrasts exotoxins with endotoxin.
objectives: Explain why Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria stain differently, and why mycobacteria need an acid-fast stain.
Distinguish colonisation, infection and opportunistic infection.
Explain the steps of bacterial pathogenesis using named virulence factors.
Distinguish exotoxins, superantigens and endotoxin by source and mechanism.
Interpret a Gram stain and simple bench tests to narrow down an organism.

sections.body:
Bacteria are single cells with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Each structure has a consequence for staining, virulence or drug targeting.
- Chromosome: a single circular DNA molecule, often with plasmids (small DNA circles) that can carry toxin or antibiotic-resistance genes and pass between bacteria.
- Ribosomes: 70S (50S + 30S subunits), unlike our 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes, so several antibiotics can target them selectively.
- Cell wall: peptidoglycan (sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides), which human cells lack. Mycoplasma has no wall at all.
- Outer membrane: present in Gram-negative bacteria only, containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
- Optional extras: a capsule (usually polysaccharide), flagella for movement, pili or fimbriae for attachment, and in Bacillus, Clostridium and Clostridioides, spores that resist heat and disinfectants.

Many bacteria live harmlessly on us as commensals and protect us by competing with pathogens. Colonisation means organisms are present without harm or a host response; infection means they invade and cause damage or a host response. Opportunists cause disease mainly when defences are weakened.
Pathogenesis usually follows four steps:
- Entry and adhesion: pili and other adhesins bind host cells, for example fimbriae of Escherichia coli binding urinary tract epithelium.
- Invasion and spread: enzymes break down tissue; some bacteria survive inside cells.
- Evasion: a capsule resists phagocytosis and complement; Staphylococcus aureus protein A binds the Fc part of antibodies; some bacteria cleave IgA.
- Damage: by toxins and by the host's own inflammatory response.
Koch's postulates (late 19th century) set out criteria for linking a microbe to a disease, but they fail for organisms that cannot be cultured and for asymptomatic carriers.

- Exotoxins are proteins secreted by bacteria, often with highly specific targets.
- Tetanus toxin (Clostridium tetani) blocks release of inhibitory transmitters (glycine and GABA) from spinal interneurons, so muscles contract unchecked: spastic paralysis.
- Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction: flaccid paralysis.
- Cholera toxin locks a G protein in its active state, raising cAMP in gut cells, so chloride and water pour into the lumen as watery diarrhoea.
- Diphtheria toxin stops protein synthesis.
- Superantigens such as toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 link MHC class II to T-cell receptors outside the peptide-binding site, activating very many T cells at once and causing a cytokine storm.
- Endotoxin is lipid A of LPS in the Gram-negative outer membrane. It is released when bacteria die or divide, is recognised by Toll-like receptor 4, and triggers cytokines that cause fever and, in large amounts, septic shock.

- Gram stain: crystal violet, then iodine, then a decolouriser (alcohol or acetone), then a red counterstain such as safranin.
- Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that keeps the violet–iodine complex, so they look purple. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin layer plus an outer membrane; the violet washes out and they take up the counterstain, so they look pink.
- Shape and arrangement narrow the possibilities: cocci in clusters suggest staphylococci, cocci in chains suggest streptococci, Gram-negative diplococci suggest Neisseria.
- Bench tests: staphylococci are catalase-positive and streptococci catalase-negative; S. aureus is coagulase-positive.
- Mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acids and stain poorly with Gram's method; they are acid-fast, shown with the Ziehl–Neelsen stain.
- Oxygen needs also help: obligate aerobes, obligate anaerobes and facultative anaerobes, which grow with or without oxygen.

A woman has fever, rigors and loin pain. A urine sample grows Gram-negative rods, later identified as E. coli. The concepts connect: fimbriae let the organism adhere to urinary epithelium and ascend despite the flushing of urine; LPS in its outer membrane is recognised by TLR4, and the resulting cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6) cause her fever and can drop blood pressure.
Compare a man with a contaminated wound who later develops jaw stiffness and spasms. Here the damage is caused by a single exotoxin (tetanus toxin) acting far from the wound, which is why toxoid vaccination protects: it induces antibody that neutralises the toxin rather than the bacterium.

- Students often think endotoxin is any toxin made by Gram-negative bacteria. In fact endotoxin means lipid A of LPS; Gram-negative bacteria also secrete exotoxins (cholera toxin is one).
- Students often think a positive culture means infection. Colonisation is common (for example skin staphylococci), so results must be read alongside the clinical picture.
- Students often think Gram-negative means the cell has no peptidoglycan. It has a thin layer; it is the outer membrane and thin wall that let the violet dye wash out.
- Students often think all bacteria can be Gram stained usefully. Mycoplasma has no wall and mycobacteria need an acid-fast stain.

notes.overview: Viruses, fungi, parasites and prions differ from bacteria in ways that decide how they are diagnosed, which immune response controls them and which drugs can reach them. Learn each agent's structure, how it enters and damages the host, and the classic examples.
objectives: Explain why viruses are obligate intracellular parasites and how receptor binding explains tissue tropism.
Describe the stages of a viral replication cycle, including reverse transcription in HIV.
Distinguish antigenic drift from antigenic shift in influenza A.
Distinguish fungi, protozoa, helminths and prions by structure and typical immune response.
Apply knowledge of the agent to predict who is at risk, such as opportunistic fungi in immunosuppression.

sections.body:
Viruses are not cells. Each has a genome of DNA or RNA (not both) inside a protein capsid; some also have a lipid envelope taken from a host cell membrane. They have no ribosomes or metabolism of their own, so they replicate only inside host cells.
- Enveloped viruses (for example influenza, HIV and herpesviruses) are generally more easily inactivated by drying, detergents and alcohol than non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus.
- Disease arises by direct killing of infected cells (HIV destroying CD4 T cells), by immune-mediated damage (much of the illness in many infections), by latency and reactivation, or by transformation: human papillomavirus contributes to cervical and other cancers, and hepatitis B and C to liver cancer.

sections.h: Replication cycle, latency and antigenic change
sections.body:
- Attachment: a viral protein binds a specific host receptor, explaining tropism. HIV gp120 binds CD4 plus a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4); influenza haemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory cells.
- Entry and uncoating by membrane fusion or endocytosis.
- Genome replication and protein synthesis on host ribosomes. HIV, a retrovirus, uses reverse transcriptase to copy RNA into DNA, which integrase inserts into the host genome.
- Assembly and release by budding (enveloped viruses) or lysis. Influenza neuraminidase cuts sialic acid so new virions escape.
Latency: herpes simplex persists in sensory ganglia and reactivates as cold sores; varicella-zoster reactivates as shingles.
Influenza A changes in two ways. Antigenic drift is gradual point mutation in haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, so seasonal vaccines are updated. Antigenic shift is reassortment of genome segments between strains (the genome is segmented), creating a new subtype that can cause a pandemic.

- Fungi are eukaryotes. Their membranes contain ergosterol rather than cholesterol, and their walls contain chitin and glucans; both are drug targets. Yeasts (Candida) are single cells; moulds (Aspergillus) grow as branching hyphae. notes.overview: Innate immunity acts within minutes to hours, needs no previous exposure and recognises broad microbial patterns. Describe the three complement pathways and the functions of C3b, C3a/C5a and the membrane attack complex.

- Barriers: intact skin, mucus and the mucociliary escalator, flushing of urine and tears; stomach acid, lysozyme and defensins; commensals that compete with pathogens (broad-spectrum antibiotics that disturb gut flora can let Clostridioides difficile take over).
- Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) absent from our cells. Toll-like receptors are the best known: TLR4 recognises LPS, TLR5 flagellin, TLR3 double-stranded RNA and TLR9 unmethylated CpG DNA. PRRs also detect damage-associated patterns, which is why sterile injury inflames.
- Neutrophils: the most numerous blood leucocytes, first to arrive in acute bacterial infection, short-lived phagocytes and the main cells in pus.
- Macrophages: phagocytes that release cytokines and present antigen. Dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.
- Natural killer cells kill cells that have lost MHC class I ('missing self'). Mast cells, basophils and eosinophils matter in allergy and anti-parasite defence.

- Complement is activated by the classical pathway (antibody bound to antigen, via C1q), the lectin pathway (mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars) and the alternative pathway (spontaneous C3 activation on microbial surfaces). All converge on C3 convertase.

- Phagocytosis: opsonins (IgG, C3b) bind phagocyte receptors; the phagosome fuses with lysosomes; NADPH oxidase produces reactive oxygen species (the respiratory burst). Its absence causes chronic granulomatous disease.

sections.h: Acute inflammation and its systemic effects
sections.body:
- Classic signs: redness, heat, swelling and pain, with loss of function added later.
- Arteriolar dilation (histamine, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) raises blood flow: redness and heat. Leaky venules let protein-rich exudate into the tissue: swelling. Bradykinin and prostaglandins sensitise nerve endings: pain.
- IL-1, TNF-α and IL-6 are endogenous pyrogens: they trigger prostaglandin E2, which raises the hypothalamic temperature set point (fever).
- IL-6 in particular drives the liver to release acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP), which can opsonise bacteria.
- Type I interferons from virus-infected cells put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state.

- White cell count and differential: bacterial infection typically raises neutrophils (neutrophilia), sometimes with immature forms; many viral infections give a normal or raised lymphocyte count; helminths raise eosinophils.
- CRP rises over hours as the liver responds to IL-6, so a very early sample can be normal; it is non-specific and also rises after trauma, surgery and in inflammatory disease.
- Lactate (on a blood gas) reflects tissue hypoperfusion in severe infection.
- Cerebrospinal fluid in meningitis follows the same logic: neutrophils with a very low glucose ratio and high protein suggest bacteria; lymphocytes with a near-normal glucose ratio suggest a virus (typical patterns; laboratory ranges differ).
- Blood cultures look for the organism itself and should be taken before antimicrobials where this does not delay urgent treatment.

sections.h: Sepsis: definition and recognition in the UK
sections.body:
Sepsis-3 (2016) defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is the subset needing vasopressors to keep mean arterial pressure at 65 mmHg or more, with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid.
In the UK, NICE NG51 (2016) has been replaced by three guidelines: NG253 (people aged 16 or over, published November 2025), NG254 (under 16s) and NG255 (pregnant or recently pregnant people). Principles from NG253, checked November 2026:
- Think 'could this be sepsis?' in anyone with signs of possible infection; do not rely on fever or hypothermia to rule it in or out.
- In acute hospitals, NEWS2 stratifies risk: 7 or more high, 5–6 moderate, 1–4 low, 0 very low. A single parameter scoring 3 needs a high-priority review and, if the infection is its likely cause, raises the level (a score of 5–6 with such a parameter is managed as high risk). A mottled or ashen appearance, a non-blanching rash or cyanosis can also raise it.
- High risk: blood tests including blood cultures and lactate, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating NEWS2. Moderate risk: antibiotics within 3 hours, but managed as high risk if there is hypoperfusion (lactate over 2 mmol/L or acute kidney injury). Low risk: within 6 hours.
- Suspect neutropenic sepsis after systemic anticancer treatment in the last 30 days.
- NICE is updating NG253 on the use of procalcitonin tests, so check for new recommendations.

notes.h: Adaptive immunity: T cells, B cells and antibodies
notes.overview: Adaptive immunity is specific and has memory, but takes days to develop on first exposure. T cells recognise peptides presented on MHC; B cells make antibodies whose class decides what they do. Knowing which cell, MHC class and antibody fits which pathogen is the key exam skill.
objectives: Explain how thymic selection produces T cells that recognise self-MHC but tolerate self-antigens.
Distinguish MHC class I and class II presentation and the T cells that read each.
Explain the three signals needed to activate a naive T cell and the roles of helper subsets.
Describe how T-cell help leads to class switching and affinity maturation.
Interpret IgM and IgG results to distinguish recent from past infection.

sections.body:
All lymphocytes arise in bone marrow. B cells mature there; T cells mature in the thymus, where positive selection keeps cells whose receptors recognise self-MHC and negative selection removes those binding self-antigens too strongly (central tolerance). Regulatory T cells add peripheral tolerance.
T cells recognise short peptides presented on MHC (HLA in humans, genes on chromosome 6), not free antigen.
- MHC class I is on almost all nucleated cells and shows peptides from inside the cell (for example viral proteins) to CD8 T cells.
- MHC class II is on professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) and shows peptides from engulfed material to CD4 T cells.
- Memory aid: CD8 × class I = 8; CD4 × class II = 8.

sections.h: Activating T cells and what they do
sections.body:
- Signal 1: the T-cell receptor binds peptide–MHC.
- Signal 2: co-stimulation, mainly CD28 on the T cell binding CD80/CD86 (B7) on the dendritic cell. Signal 1 without signal 2 tends to cause anergy.
- Signal 3: cytokines steer differentiation. The activated cell then divides (clonal expansion) into effector and memory cells.
CD4 helper subsets:
- Th1: IFN-γ, macrophage activation; key against intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria.
- Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; IgE and eosinophils against helminths; involved in allergy.
- Th17: IL-17, neutrophil recruitment; extracellular bacteria and fungi.
- T follicular helper cells help B cells in germinal centres; FOXP3-positive regulatory T cells suppress responses.
CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill infected or abnormal cells through perforin and granzymes, or Fas–Fas ligand, triggering apoptosis.

B cells carry a membrane antibody (the B-cell receptor). Protein antigens need T-cell help (T-dependent); polysaccharides can activate B cells without it (T-independent) but give little class switching or memory.
In germinal centres, CD40 ligand on helper T cells binding CD40 on B cells permits class switching; somatic hypermutation plus selection raises affinity (affinity maturation). B cells become plasma cells or memory B cells.
Antibody structure: two heavy and two light chains; Fab binds antigen, Fc decides function.
- IgM: first in a primary response; a pentamer, strong complement activator.
- IgG: most abundant in serum; crosses the placenta; opsonises and activates complement.
- IgA: dimer in secretions and breast milk, protecting mucosa.
- IgE: binds mast cells and basophils; allergy and anti-helminth defence.
- IgD: mainly on naive B cells as a receptor.
Functions: neutralisation, opsonisation, complement activation and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells.

- Primary response: a lag of about a week or more, mostly IgM at first, of lower affinity. Secondary response: faster and larger, mainly IgG of higher affinity, because memory cells exist.
- So specific IgM with little specific IgG suggests a recent first infection; IgG alone suggests past infection or vaccination.
- A rising IgG level between an early (acute) and a later (convalescent) sample also points to recent infection.
- In a young baby, IgG may be the mother's (it crosses the placenta), whereas IgM made by the baby suggests the baby's own infection.

notes.h: Immune memory, vaccination and when defences fail
notes.overview: Vaccination uses immune memory on purpose; immunodeficiency and hypersensitivity show what happens when defences are too weak or misdirected. Link each vaccine type to the response it produces, and work back from a pattern of infections to the missing component.
objectives: Distinguish active and passive immunity, with natural and artificial examples.
Explain why conjugate vaccines protect infants when plain polysaccharide vaccines do not.
Interpret a pattern of recurrent infections to identify the likely immune defect.

sections.h: Types of immunity and of vaccine
sections.body:
- Active immunity: your own response after infection or vaccination; slower, but gives memory. Passive immunity: transferred antibody, immediate but short-lived, no memory (maternal IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk, immunoglobulin products).
- Live attenuated vaccines (for example MMRV, BCG, oral rotavirus, the nasal influenza vaccine for children) give strong, long-lasting antibody and T-cell responses but are generally avoided in significant immunosuppression and in pregnancy.
- Inactivated whole organisms (inactivated polio), toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria) and subunit or recombinant proteins (hepatitis B surface antigen, HPV virus-like particles) cannot cause the infection but usually need adjuvants (such as aluminium salts) and boosters.
- mRNA and viral-vector vaccines, used widely against COVID-19, deliver instructions so the body makes the antigen.

Plain capsular polysaccharides are T-independent antigens: they cross-link B-cell receptors without T-cell help, giving weak responses in children under about two and little memory. Conjugate vaccines join the polysaccharide to a carrier protein; polysaccharide-specific B cells take up the conjugate and present carrier peptides to helper T cells, so the response becomes T-dependent, with class switching and memory, even in infants (Hib, pneumococcal and MenACWY conjugates).
Gell and Coombs (1963) classify hypersensitivity:
- Type I: IgE on mast cells cross-linked by allergen, histamine within minutes (hay fever, anaphylaxis).
- Type II: antibody against cell or tissue antigens (haemolytic transfusion reaction, Goodpasture's disease).
- Type III: immune complexes deposited in tissues (serum sickness, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, SLE).
- Type IV: delayed, T-cell mediated, peaking after one to three days (contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test).

- Antibody or complement defects: recurrent bacterial infections, especially with encapsulated organisms. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK mutation, no mature B cells) usually presents after about 6 months of age, once maternal IgG wanes.
- T-cell defects: viral, fungal and intracellular infections. DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) reduces thymic T-cell output; severe combined immunodeficiency affects both arms.
- Neutrophil defects: bacterial and fungal infections (chronic granulomatous disease, neutropenia after chemotherapy).
- After splenectomy: risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcus).
- Secondary causes are far commoner than inherited ones: HIV, chemotherapy and other immunosuppressive drugs, malnutrition and diabetes.

sections.h: CD4 counts and hepatitis B serology
sections.body:
- HIV infects CD4 T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells; untreated, the CD4 count falls over years. The US CDC surveillance definition (2014), widely used in teaching, classes HIV as stage 3 (AIDS) when the CD4 count is below 200 cells per microlitre in people aged 6 or over, or when an AIDS-defining illness such as Pneumocystis pneumonia occurs. Effective combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus and lets the CD4 count recover.

notes.h: Epidemiology, transmission and control of infection
notes.overview: The epidemiology of infection asks who gets infected, how it spreads and how spread can be stopped. Learn the chain of infection, the arithmetic of R0 and herd immunity, the shape of epidemic curves, and the legal and practical steps used to control infection in England.
objectives: Explain the chain of infection and how each control measure breaks a link.
Calculate effective R and the herd immunity threshold, and adjust for vaccine effectiveness.
Distinguish incidence from prevalence, and point-source from propagated outbreaks.
Apply the notification duty and standard infection control precautions to a clinical scenario.

sections.h: The chain of infection and modes of transmission
sections.body:
Chain of infection: agent, reservoir (people, animals, environment), portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Control breaks one or more links.
- Contact: direct (touch, sexual contact) or indirect via hands and contaminated objects (fomites).
- Respiratory: traditionally split into large droplets that fall within about a metre and small airborne particles that stay suspended and travel further (measles, tuberculosis). Many experts now describe a spectrum of particle sizes; how much each contributes for a given infection is still debated.
- Faecal–oral: food, water or hands (norovirus, hepatitis A).
- Vector-borne: insects such as mosquitoes (malaria).
- Blood-borne: needles and transfusion (hepatitis B and C, HIV).
- Vertical: mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.

sections.h: R0, effective R and herd immunity
sections.body:
- The basic reproduction number R0 is the average number of secondary cases from one case in a fully susceptible population. It depends on the organism, contact patterns and setting, so published values are ranges.
- In the simplest model, effective R ≈ R0 × proportion still susceptible. An epidemic grows while R > 1 and declines when R < 1.
- Herd immunity threshold H = 1 − 1/R0. If R0 = 10, H = 1 − 0.1 = 0.9: about 90% must be immune.
- No vaccine is 100% effective, so coverage needed = H ÷ vaccine effectiveness. With R0 = 10 and a vaccine 95% effective: 0.9 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 0.947, about 95%.
- Measles R0 is often quoted as 12–18 (published estimates vary more widely), giving thresholds of 1 − 1/12 ≈ 0.92 to 1 − 1/18 ≈ 0.94, which is why very high vaccine coverage is needed.

- Incubation period: from infection to first symptoms. Infectious period: when a person can transmit, which can begin before symptoms.
- Carrier: an infected person who transmits without symptoms.
- Endemic: constantly present in a population. Epidemic: more cases than expected. Pandemic: an epidemic across several countries or continents. Outbreak: two or more linked cases, or more cases than expected in one place.
- Incidence: new cases in a period. Prevalence: all existing cases at a time. A long-lasting disease can have high prevalence despite low incidence.
- Case fatality ratio: deaths among people with the disease divided by the number of cases.

- Confirm the outbreak and the diagnosis (clinical details, samples).
- Write a case definition (who counts, when and where) and find cases actively.
- Plot an epidemic curve. A single sharp peak about one incubation period after exposure suggests a point source (for example one contaminated meal); successive, rising waves suggest person-to-person (propagated) spread.
- Compare exposures of ill and well people to find the likely vehicle.
- Control: remove the source, isolate cases, trace and advise contacts, and offer vaccination or post-exposure prophylaxis where appropriate (for example, UKHSA guidance offers human normal immunoglobulin, a form of passive immunity, to susceptible pregnant women and infants exposed to measles, ideally within 72 hours).

sections.h: Notification and infection control in England
sections.body:
Checked November 2026:
- Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, a registered medical practitioner must notify on suspicion of a notifiable disease, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. UKHSA asks for urgent cases to be phoned to the local health protection team within 24 hours, and all cases reported through its online service within 3 days. Laboratories separately notify specified causative agents.
- The list was expanded from 6 April 2025 (for example chickenpox and CJD were added) and hantavirus disease was added in 2026; it includes measles, acute meningitis, meningococcal septicaemia, tuberculosis and food poisoning.
- Standard infection control precautions apply to every patient, including hand hygiene, PPE, safe sharps and a clean care environment; transmission-based precautions are added for specific infections.
- Hand hygiene moments: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings. Use soap and water rather than alcohol rub when hands are visibly soiled and for vomiting, diarrhoea or suspected C. difficile or norovirus.

Fifteen guests develop vomiting and diarrhoea within a day and a half of a wedding meal. A sharp single peak on the epidemic curve points to a point source. Comparing what ill and well guests ate identifies the likely dish; stool samples confirm the organism. Food poisoning is notifiable, and urgent when part of a cluster or outbreak, so the doctor who suspects it phones the health protection team. Ill kitchen staff are excluded until no longer infectious, and staff and guests are advised to wash hands with soap and water, because alcohol rub is less reliable against norovirus.

- Students often think the herd immunity threshold is the vaccine coverage target. The threshold is about immunity; coverage must be higher when the vaccine is less than fully effective.
- Students often think notification waits for a positive test. The legal duty applies on suspicion.
- Students often think R0 is a fixed property of a microbe. It varies with contact patterns and setting, and effective R falls as immunity rises.
- Students often think gloves replace hand hygiene. Hands are cleaned before putting gloves on and after removing them.

notes.h: Social and psychological effects of infection on patients
notes.overview: UCL's description of Infection and Defence includes the social and psychological consequences of infection. Infection can change how people see themselves, how others treat them, and whether they seek and stay in care. Stigma, the sick role, social determinants and confidentiality all shape outcomes.
objectives: Explain stigma using Goffman's definition and Link and Phelan's components.
Describe the psychological effects of infection and of isolation for infection control.
Explain how social conditions raise the risk of infections such as tuberculosis and delay diagnosis.
Apply GMC confidentiality principles and the notification duty to a scenario.
Distinguish the three Cs of vaccine hesitancy and respond to each.

sections.body:
Erving Goffman (Stigma, 1963) described stigma as a deeply discrediting attribute that reduces a person, in others' eyes, from a whole person to a tainted one. Link and Phelan (2001) describe stigma as labelling, stereotyping, separation, status loss and discrimination occurring together in a situation where power allows them.
- Infections with a long history of stigma include HIV, tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C, sexually transmitted infections and leprosy; outbreaks such as COVID-19 and mpox have been accompanied by blame of particular groups.
- Effects: delay in testing and seeking care, reluctance to tell partners or family, poorer adherence, loss of work or relationships, shame and depression.
- Accurate counter-messages help. In the PARTNER studies there were no within-couple sexual transmissions when the partner with HIV had a suppressed viral load on treatment, the basis of the 'Undetectable = Untransmittable' (U=U) message.

- Poverty, overcrowding, homelessness, imprisonment and poor housing raise the risk of infections such as tuberculosis. In England in 2025, the TB notification rate in the most deprived tenth of the population was 19.4 per 100,000 against 2.8 in the least deprived, and 16.7% of people with TB had at least one social risk factor (alcohol or drug misuse, homelessness, imprisonment, mental health needs or asylum seeker status).
- Barriers to care (difficulty registering with a GP, fear of charges or immigration checks) can delay diagnosis; the median delay from symptoms to diagnosis of pulmonary TB in England was 74 days in 2025.
- Occupation matters: healthcare workers, people who work with animals and sex workers face particular risks.
- Infection can also push people into hardship through lost earnings during illness or isolation and caring responsibilities.

sections.h: Psychological effects and the sick role
sections.body:
- Anxiety about the illness, about infecting others and about the future; depression, especially with chronic infection, disfigurement or long illness.
- Isolation for infection control: a 2020 systematic review of mainly observational studies linked it with higher depression and anxiety scores, less clinician contact and more adverse events such as falls; causation cannot be proven, but isolated patients need deliberate attention.
- Severe infection can cause delirium, especially in older people.
- Talcott Parsons (The Social System, 1951) described the sick role: the sick person is exempt from normal duties and not blamed for being ill, but is obliged to want to recover and to seek and cooperate with competent help. Critics question its relevance to long-term illness, and stigmatised illnesses are often blamed on the patient, breaking its assumptions.

Checked November 2026:
- Statutory notification of notifiable diseases is a legal duty, which does not need consent.
- GMC guidance: encourage patients to tell people at risk (for example sexual partners) and explain how to protect them. Disclosure without consent can be justified in the public interest when failing to disclose may expose others to a risk of death or serious harm; tell the patient before disclosing where practicable and safe, disclose the minimum necessary and record the decision.
- Measures that restrict individuals (isolation, exclusion from work or school, contact tracing) raise ethical questions about liberty, confidentiality and fairness; they work better with explanation and practical support.
- Vaccine hesitancy is delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite available services. The WHO SAGE working group describes confidence (trust in vaccines and the system), complacency (low perceived risk) and convenience (access). Listening and giving clear, honest information works better than dismissing concerns.

A student is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. She fears housemates will see her as dirty, worries she has infected them, and must stay away from university during the infectious period. Treatment lasts months and disrupts study and income. Each strand matters clinically: stigma and isolation can lower mood, low mood can reduce adherence, and poor adherence risks relapse and drug resistance. Good care names these fears, explains how TB spreads and when she stops being infectious, arranges practical support, and involves the TB service in contact tracing so that she does not have to tell everyone herself.

- Students often think isolation is harmless because it protects others. It can bring anxiety, fewer clinician visits and adverse events.

notes.h: How antimicrobial drugs act, resistance and stewardship
notes.overview: This topic covers how anti-infective drugs work in principle, how microbes become resistant and how UK stewardship aims to keep antimicrobials working. It does not cover prescribing or doses, which always come from current local guidelines and the BNF.
objectives: Explain selective toxicity using named antibacterial targets.
Explain how resistance arises and spreads, with a named mechanism for each main type.
Interpret a broth dilution series to find the MIC.
Distinguish bactericidal from bacteriostatic action and narrow from broad spectrum.
Apply Start smart then focus to a patient at the 48–72 hour review.

sections.body:
A good antimicrobial hits a target the microbe has and we lack, or one that differs enough to be hit selectively.
- Cell wall: β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and stop peptidoglycan cross-linking. Glycopeptides such as vancomycin bind the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of wall precursors; they are too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane.
- 70S ribosome: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on the 30S subunit, macrolides on the 50S. Aminoglycosides need oxygen-dependent uptake, so they do not work against anaerobes.
- Nucleic acids: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; metronidazole is activated in anaerobic organisms and damages their DNA.
- Folate: sulfonamides block dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim dihydrofolate reductase; bacteria must make folate, whereas we absorb it.
- Membranes: polymyxins (colistin) bind LPS and disrupt the outer and inner membranes of Gram-negative bacteria.

sections.h: Resistance: how it arises and spreads
sections.body:
- Intrinsic resistance is natural (the outer membrane keeping vancomycin out of Gram-negatives). Acquired resistance arises by mutation or by gaining genes.
- Gene transfer: conjugation (plasmids passed through a pilus), transformation (uptake of free DNA) and transduction (bacteriophages). Plasmids can carry several resistance genes, so one transfer can confer multidrug resistance.
- Mechanisms: enzymes that destroy the drug (β-lactamases, extended-spectrum β-lactamases, carbapenemases); altered targets (MRSA's mecA gene encodes PBP2a, which β-lactams bind poorly; vancomycin-resistant enterococci change D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac); reduced entry (porin loss); and efflux pumps.
- Every antimicrobial use selects for resistant organisms, including in normal flora, so unnecessary or unduly broad use matters. Resistant organisms spread between patients, the community, animals and the environment (One Health).

- Antivirals target steps unique to the virus. Aciclovir is activated by herpesvirus thymidine kinase, so it acts mainly in infected cells and then stops viral DNA synthesis. Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir) stop influenza release. HIV is treated with combinations acting on reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase, which makes resistance much less likely.
- Antifungals exploit fungal differences: azoles block ergosterol synthesis; polyenes (amphotericin, nystatin) bind ergosterol and form pores; echinocandins block β-glucan synthesis in the wall.
- Because fungi and protozoa are eukaryotes like us, finding selective targets is harder than for bacteria, which partly explains the side-effects of some antifungal drugs.

- Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC): the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth in the laboratory. In a doubling dilution series, it is the first clear tube.
- Minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC): the lowest concentration that kills the organism, found by subculturing clear tubes onto drug-free agar.
- Disc diffusion: the size of the zone of inhibition around an antibiotic disc is compared with standard breakpoints.
- Bactericidal drugs kill; bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and rely on host defences. The distinction depends on organism and concentration and matters most where defences are weak (endocarditis, meningitis, neutropenia).
- Killing pattern: β-lactams depend mainly on time above the MIC, aminoglycosides mainly on peak concentration.
- Spectrum: broad-spectrum drugs disturb normal flora more, raising the risk of C. difficile and of selecting resistance.

Checked November 2026:
- NICE NG15 (August 2015; only links updated since) sets out organisational systems for stewardship.

- Review at 48–72 hours and record one of five decisions: cease, amend (usually narrower), refer (for example to outpatient or virtual-ward care), extend with a stop or review date, or switch from intravenous to oral.
- NICE NG253 (sepsis, 2025) likewise asks for antibiotics to be reviewed and narrowed once the source or microbiology is known.

notes.body:
Selective toxicity and antibacterial targets
A good antimicrobial hits a target the microbe has and we lack, or one that differs enough to be hit selectively.
- Cell wall: β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and stop peptidoglycan cross-linking. Glycopeptides such as vancomycin bind the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of wall precursors; they are too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane.
- 70S ribosome: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on the 30S subunit, macrolides on the 50S. Aminoglycosides need oxygen-dependent uptake, so they do not work against anaerobes.
- Nucleic acids: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; metronidazole is activated in anaerobic organisms and damages their DNA.
- Folate: sulfonamides block dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim dihydrofolate reductase; bacteria must make folate, whereas we absorb it.
- Membranes: polymyxins (colistin) bind LPS and disrupt the outer and inner membranes of Gram-negative bacteria.

Resistance: how it arises and spreads
- Intrinsic resistance is natural (the outer membrane keeping vancomycin out of Gram-negatives). Acquired resistance arises by mutation or by gaining genes.
- Gene transfer: conjugation (plasmids passed through a pilus), transformation (uptake of free DNA) and transduction (bacteriophages). Plasmids can carry several resistance genes, so one transfer can confer multidrug resistance.
- Mechanisms: enzymes that destroy the drug (β-lactamases, extended-spectrum β-lactamases, carbapenemases); altered targets (MRSA's mecA gene encodes PBP2a, which β-lactams bind poorly; vancomycin-resistant enterococci change D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac); reduced entry (porin loss); and efflux pumps.
- Every antimicrobial use selects for resistant organisms, including in normal flora, so unnecessary or unduly broad use matters. Resistant organisms spread between patients, the community, animals and the environment (One Health).

Antivirals and antifungals
- Antivirals target steps unique to the virus. Aciclovir is activated by herpesvirus thymidine kinase, so it acts mainly in infected cells and then stops viral DNA synthesis. Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir) stop influenza release. HIV is treated with combinations acting on reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase, which makes resistance much less likely.
- Antifungals exploit fungal differences: azoles block ergosterol synthesis; polyenes (amphotericin, nystatin) bind ergosterol and form pores; echinocandins block β-glucan synthesis in the wall.
- Because fungi and protozoa are eukaryotes like us, finding selective targets is harder than for bacteria, which partly explains the side-effects of some antifungal drugs.

Measuring susceptibility
- Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC): the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth in the laboratory. In a doubling dilution series, it is the first clear tube.
- Minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC): the lowest concentration that kills the organism, found by subculturing clear tubes onto drug-free agar.
- Disc diffusion: the size of the zone of inhibition around an antibiotic disc is compared with standard breakpoints.
- Bactericidal drugs kill; bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and rely on host defences. The distinction depends on organism and concentration and matters most where defences are weak (endocarditis, meningitis, neutropenia).
- Killing pattern: β-lactams depend mainly on time above the MIC, aminoglycosides mainly on peak concentration.
- Spectrum: broad-spectrum drugs disturb normal flora more, raising the risk of C. difficile and of selecting resistance.

Antimicrobial stewardship in the UK
Checked November 2026:
- NICE NG15 (August 2015; only links updated since) sets out organisational systems for stewardship.
- UKHSA's Start smart then focus (updated September 2023): start only with clear evidence of infection; take cultures before antimicrobials where possible, but do not delay prompt treatment of severe sepsis or life-threatening infection; follow local guidelines; document the indication, severity and a duration or review date.
- Review at 48–72 hours and record one of five decisions: cease, amend (usually narrower), refer (for example to outpatient or virtual-ward care), extend with a stop or review date, or switch from intravenous to oral.
- NICE NG253 (sepsis, 2025) likewise asks for antibiotics to be reviewed and narrowed once the source or microbiology is known.
- The UK national action plan 2024–2029 aims to cut total human antibiotic use by 5% from the 2019–20 baseline by 2029, and for 70% of use to come from the Access category of the UK-AWaRe classification.
- Choice of drug and dose always comes from current local guidelines and the BNF; none are given in this pack.

- Students often think a lower MIC always means a better drug. MICs are compared with each drug's own breakpoints and with what the drug can achieve at the site of infection.

cards.f: Why do Gram-positive bacteria stain purple?
cards.b: Their thick peptidoglycan wall keeps the crystal violet–iodine complex during decolourising. Gram-negatives (thin peptidoglycan plus outer membrane) lose it and take up the red counterstain.
cards.ex: The stain difference is a wall-structure difference: thick wall traps dye, thin wall plus outer membrane lets it wash out.

cards.f: Why can some antibiotics target bacterial ribosomes without stopping human protein synthesis?
cards.b: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S subunits); human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, so drugs binding bacterial subunits can act selectively.
cards.ex: Selective toxicity depends on a structural difference between microbe and host.

cards.f: Exotoxin vs endotoxin
cards.b: Exotoxins: proteins secreted by Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria, often very specific. Endotoxin: lipid A of LPS in the Gram-negative outer membrane, recognised by TLR4.
cards.ex: Ask: is it a secreted protein (exotoxin) or part of the outer membrane (endotoxin)?

cards.f: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive: likely organism?
cards.b: Staphylococcus aureus. Clusters and a positive catalase test point to staphylococci; coagulase positivity singles out S. aureus.
cards.ex: Chains plus catalase-negative would point to streptococci instead.

cards.f: Why does Mycobacterium tuberculosis need a Ziehl–Neelsen stain?
cards.b: Its wall is rich in waxy mycolic acids, so it takes up Gram stain poorly; once stained it resists acid–alcohol decolourising (acid-fast).
cards.ex: Mycolic acids are the reason for both the poor Gram stain and the acid-fast property.

cards.f: How does a superantigen cause toxic shock?
cards.b: It links MHC class II to T-cell receptors outside the peptide groove, activating very many T cells at once, causing massive cytokine release.
cards.ex: Normal antigens activate a tiny fraction of T cells; superantigens bypass peptide specificity.

cards.f: Colonisation vs infection
cards.b: Colonisation: organisms present and multiplying without harm or host response. Infection: invasion causing tissue damage or a host response.
cards.ex: A positive swab alone does not prove infection; look for damage or a host response.

cards.f: Spastic paralysis after a dirty wound: which toxin mechanism?
cards.b: Tetanus toxin blocks release of inhibitory transmitters (glycine, GABA) from spinal interneurons, so motor neurons fire unchecked.
cards.ex: Botulinum toxin gives the opposite (flaccid) picture by blocking acetylcholine release.

cards.f: Why are viruses obligate intracellular parasites?
cards.b: They lack ribosomes and their own metabolism, so they can make proteins and copy their genomes only inside a host cell.
cards.ex: No ribosomes means no protein synthesis without a host.

cards.f: Antigenic drift vs shift (influenza A)
cards.b: Drift: gradual point mutations in haemagglutinin/neuraminidase (seasonal epidemics). Shift: reassortment of genome segments creating a new subtype (pandemic risk).
cards.ex: Shift by reassortment needs a segmented genome and co-infection of one cell with two strains.

cards.f: How does HIV enter and persist in CD4 T cells?
cards.b: gp120 binds CD4 plus CCR5 or CXCR4; after fusion, reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into DNA, which integrase inserts into the host genome.
cards.ex: Integration explains why HIV persists and cannot simply be cleared.

cards.f: Site of herpes simplex latency
cards.b: Sensory nerve ganglia; the virus reactivates to cause recurrent lesions such as cold sores.
cards.ex: Herpesviruses persist for life; varicella-zoster reactivates as shingles.

cards.f: Why is ergosterol a useful antifungal target?
cards.b: Fungal membranes use ergosterol where human cells use cholesterol, so azoles (block synthesis) and polyenes (bind it) act selectively.
cards.ex: Fungi are eukaryotes, so selective targets are scarce; ergosterol is one of the few.

cards.f: Returned traveller with blood eosinophilia: which kind of organism is most likely?
cards.b: A helminth (worm). Worms are too large to engulf and drive a Th2 response with IL-5, IgE and eosinophils.
cards.ex: Bacterial infection typically raises neutrophils; many viral infections raise lymphocytes.

cards.f: Instruments used on a patient later found to have CJD: why is standard sterilisation a problem?
cards.b: Prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid and resist standard sterilisation, so special handling or disposal is needed.
cards.ex: Methods that destroy nucleic acids or microbes do not reliably destroy prions.

cards.f: Pneumocystis jirovecii: what kind of organism, and who gets it?
cards.b: A fungus (once thought to be a protozoan) causing pneumonia mainly in people with very low CD4 counts, such as advanced HIV.
cards.ex: It is a classic opportunist of T-cell deficiency.

cards.f: PAMP
cards.b: Pathogen-associated molecular pattern: a structure shared by many microbes but absent from host cells (e.g. LPS, flagellin), recognised by pattern recognition receptors.
cards.ex: PRRs recognise patterns, not specific antigens.

cards.f: Functions of C3b, C5a and C5b–C9
cards.b: C3b: opsonin. C5a (and C3a): anaphylatoxin, increases permeability; C5a attracts neutrophils. C5b–C9: membrane attack complex.
cards.ex: Think 'coat, call, kill': C3b coats, C5a calls, C5b–C9 kills.

cards.f: Steps of neutrophil recruitment
cards.b: Rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins binding ICAM-1), transmigration between endothelial cells, then chemotaxis (e.g. IL-8, C5a).
cards.ex: Selectins slow; integrins stop; chemokines steer.

cards.f: Why does chronic granulomatous disease cause recurrent bacterial and fungal infections?
cards.b: Phagocyte NADPH oxidase is defective, so there is no respiratory burst and engulfed microbes are not killed effectively.
cards.ex: Phagocytes can engulf but not kill: the defect is after ingestion.

cards.f: How does infection cause fever?
cards.b: IL-1, TNF-α and IL-6 act as endogenous pyrogens; they trigger prostaglandin E2, which raises the hypothalamic temperature set point.
cards.ex: The body defends a higher set point, so you feel cold and shiver while temperature rises.

cards.f: Why does CRP rise in infection, and why can an early CRP be normal?
cards.b: IL-6 drives the liver to make acute-phase proteins including CRP; this takes hours, so CRP lags behind the start of inflammation.
cards.ex: CRP is a downstream, delayed marker, not an instant one.

cards.f: CSF: high white cells (mostly neutrophils), high protein, very low CSF:plasma glucose ratio. Likely cause?
cards.b: Bacterial meningitis. Viral meningitis typically gives lymphocytes, mildly raised protein and a normal or slightly low glucose ratio.
cards.ex: Neutrophils plus low glucose is the bacterial pattern (typical features; lab ranges differ).

cards.f: Adult in ED with suspected infection and NEWS2 of 8: what does NICE NG253 advise?
cards.b: High risk: urgent clinical assessment, blood cultures and lactate, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating NEWS2 (checked November 2026).
cards.ex: NEWS2 7 or more is the high-risk band in acute hospitals under NG253; a score of 5–6 with a single parameter scoring 3, likely caused by the infection, is also managed as high risk.

cards.f: MHC class I vs class II
cards.b: Class I: almost all nucleated cells, presents intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells. Class II: professional APCs, presents peptides from engulfed material to CD4 T cells.
cards.ex: CD8 × I = 8; CD4 × II = 8.

cards.f: Why does signal 1 without signal 2 tend to make a T cell anergic?
cards.b: Without co-stimulation (CD28 binding CD80/CD86), antigen recognition alone switches the cell off, which helps keep T cells tolerant of self-antigens on ordinary tissues.
cards.ex: Co-stimulation is a 'danger' check supplied by activated dendritic cells.

cards.f: Th1 vs Th2 vs Th17
cards.b: Th1: IFN-γ, macrophage activation (intracellular pathogens). Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IgE and eosinophils (helminths). Th17: IL-17, neutrophil recruitment (extracellular bacteria, fungi).
cards.ex: Match each subset to the pathogen it handles best.

cards.f: Which antibody crosses the placenta, and which is first in a primary response?
cards.b: IgG crosses the placenta. IgM, a pentamer that activates complement well, is made first in a primary response.
cards.ex: IgM early and big; IgG later, smaller, mobile.

cards.f: Main antibody in mucosal secretions and breast milk
cards.b: IgA, secreted as a dimer.
cards.ex: IgA protects surfaces such as gut and airway lining.

cards.f: What does class switching need, and what does it change?
cards.b: Helper T-cell CD40 ligand binding CD40 on the B cell, plus cytokines, mainly in germinal centres. It changes the Fc (constant) region, not the antigen-binding site.
cards.ex: Same specificity, new function.

cards.f: High specific IgM with little specific IgG: interpretation?
cards.b: Recent (current) primary infection. Past infection or vaccination would show mainly IgG; maternal antibody is IgG, not IgM.
cards.ex: IgM comes first in a primary response and fades.

cards.f: How do CD8 T cells kill infected cells?
cards.b: By releasing perforin and granzymes, or via Fas–Fas ligand, triggering apoptosis of the target cell.
cards.ex: They induce controlled cell death, limiting spread of virus.

cards.f: Active vs passive immunity
cards.b: Active: own immune response (infection or vaccine), slower but with memory. Passive: transferred antibody (maternal IgG, immunoglobulin), immediate, short-lived, no memory.
cards.ex: Memory needs your own B and T cells to respond.

cards.f: Why do conjugate vaccines work in infants?
cards.b: Joining capsular polysaccharide to a protein lets helper T cells be recruited, turning a weak T-independent response into a T-dependent one with class switching and memory.
cards.ex: Polysaccharides cannot be presented on MHC class II; the carrier protein can.

cards.f: Why are live attenuated vaccines generally avoided in significant immunosuppression?
cards.b: The weakened organism replicates; without adequate immunity it can spread and cause disease. Inactivated vaccines cannot replicate.
cards.ex: The strength of live vaccines (replication) is also their risk.

cards.f: Recurrent pneumonias in a boy from about 6 months, absent B cells: likely diagnosis?
cards.b: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK mutation): no mature B cells, so infections with encapsulated bacteria start as maternal IgG wanes.
cards.ex: Antibody defects show up after maternal IgG fades from about 6 months of age.

cards.f: Which infections threaten someone after splenectomy, and why?
cards.b: Encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcus), because the spleen helps clear opsonised encapsulated organisms from blood.
cards.ex: Capsules resist phagocytosis unless antibody and complement coat them.

cards.f: Gell and Coombs types I–IV
cards.b: I: IgE, immediate. II: antibody against cell or tissue antigens. III: immune complexes. IV: delayed, T-cell mediated.
cards.ex: Only type IV is cell-mediated; only type I is IgE.

cards.f: Hepatitis B serology: anti-HBs detected, anti-HBc and HBsAg not detected. Meaning?
cards.b: Immunity from vaccination. The vaccine contains surface antigen only; natural infection would also produce anti-HBc.
cards.ex: Anti-HBc is the marker of natural infection, past or present.

cards.f: Why is the newborn SCID screening result checked before rotavirus vaccine?
cards.b: Rotavirus vaccine is live; a baby with severe combined immunodeficiency could be harmed by the replicating vaccine virus (Green Book schedule, checked November 2026).
cards.ex: Live vaccines are the ones that matter in severe immunodeficiency.

cards.f: Herd immunity threshold formula
cards.b: H = 1 − 1/R0 (simple homogeneous model). Coverage needed = H ÷ vaccine effectiveness.
cards.ex: The threshold is about immunity; coverage must be higher if the vaccine is imperfect.

cards.f: R0 = 4 and 60% are immune: effective R?
cards.b: R ≈ 4 × (1 − 0.6) = 4 × 0.4 = 1.6, so cases still rise.
cards.ex: Multiply by the proportion susceptible, not the proportion immune.

cards.f: R0 = 15, vaccine 95% effective: coverage needed?
cards.ex: Work out the threshold first, then divide by effectiveness.

cards.f: Incidence vs prevalence
cards.b: Incidence: new cases over a period. Prevalence: all existing cases at a point or over a period; long-lasting diseases accumulate prevalence.
cards.ex: Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration in a steady state.

cards.f: A doctor suspects measles but results are pending. When should it be notified?
cards.b: Now, on suspicion: measles is notifiable and urgent, so phone the local health protection team (within 24 hours) and report online within 3 days (checked November 2026).
cards.ex: The legal duty is triggered by suspicion, not laboratory confirmation.

cards.f: Epidemic curve with one sharp peak vs successive rising waves
cards.b: One sharp peak about one incubation period after exposure: point source. Successive rising waves: person-to-person (propagated) spread.
cards.ex: The shape tells you whether exposure was simultaneous or chained.

cards.f: Why use soap and water rather than alcohol rub for C. difficile?
cards.b: Alcohol rub does not kill its spores; washing removes them physically. Soap and water is also used for norovirus, diarrhoea and visibly soiled hands.
cards.ex: Spores resist alcohol; mechanical removal works.

cards.f: The five moments for hand hygiene
cards.b: Before touching a patient; before a clean/aseptic procedure; after body fluid exposure risk; after touching a patient; after touching the patient's surroundings.
cards.ex: Two 'befores' protect the patient; three 'afters' protect you and the environment.

cards.f: Goffman's definition of stigma (1963)
cards.b: An attribute that deeply discredits a person, reducing them in others' eyes from a whole person to a tainted, discounted one.
cards.ex: Link and Phelan later added labelling, stereotyping, separation, status loss and discrimination where power allows.

cards.f: A man refuses HIV treatment because workmates might find out. Which concept?
cards.b: Anticipated stigma: fear of being labelled and discriminated against if the diagnosis is known, a recognised barrier to testing and treatment.
cards.ex: Focus on what he fears others will do, not on his illness behaviour.

cards.f: How does U=U counter HIV stigma?
cards.b: PARTNER studies found no within-couple sexual transmission when the partner with HIV had a suppressed viral load, so treatment both protects health and prevents transmission.
cards.ex: Accurate information reduces fear-based stigma.

cards.f: Parsons' sick role: rights vs obligations
cards.b: Rights: exemption from normal duties and from blame. Obligations: want to get well; seek and cooperate with competent help.
cards.ex: Critics question its fit with long-term illness.

cards.f: Why do patients in infection-control isolation need extra attention?
cards.b: Mainly observational studies link isolation with more anxiety and depression, less clinician contact and more adverse events such as falls.
cards.ex: Isolation protects others but can harm the isolated patient.

cards.f: TB notification rate 19.4 vs 2.8 per 100,000 in the most vs least deprived tenth (England 2025): what does it show?
cards.b: Rates were about 7 times higher in the most deprived tenth (19.4 ÷ 2.8 ≈ 6.9), showing that social conditions shape infection risk.
cards.ex: Divide the two rates to express the gap as a ratio.

cards.f: Three Cs of vaccine hesitancy
cards.b: Confidence (trust in vaccines and the system), complacency (low perceived risk), convenience (access).
cards.ex: Each needs a different response: information, risk explanation, easier access.

cards.f: A patient with HIV refuses to tell a regular sexual partner. What does GMC guidance allow?
cards.b: Encourage and support disclosure first. If others may face risk of death or serious harm, disclosure without consent can be justified in the public interest; tell the patient first where safe.
cards.ex: Confidentiality is important but not absolute (checked November 2026).

cards.f: How do β-lactams kill bacteria?
cards.b: They bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and block peptidoglycan cross-linking, weakening the wall so the cell lyses.
cards.ex: No peptidoglycan in human cells means selective toxicity.

cards.f: Why does vancomycin not work on Gram-negative bacteria?
cards.b: It is too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane to reach its D-Ala-D-Ala target.
cards.ex: This is intrinsic resistance: a property of the organism, not acquired.

cards.f: Mechanism of MRSA resistance
cards.b: The mecA gene encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for β-lactams, so wall synthesis continues.
cards.ex: Altered target, not β-lactamase.

cards.f: Broth tubes 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 mg/L: growth up to 1 mg/L, clear from 2 mg/L. MIC?
cards.b: 2 mg/L: the lowest concentration with no visible growth (the first clear tube).
cards.ex: Not the highest concentration with growth, and not the highest tested.

cards.f: Conjugation vs transformation vs transduction
cards.b: Conjugation: plasmid passed through a pilus. Transformation: uptake of free DNA. Transduction: DNA carried by a bacteriophage.
cards.ex: All are horizontal gene transfer, spreading resistance between bacteria.

cards.f: Start smart then focus at 48–72 h: improving patient, sensitive organism on culture. Decision?
cards.b: Amend to a narrower-spectrum agent (and switch IV to oral when criteria are met), documenting a stop or review date (checked November 2026).
cards.ex: The five outcomes: cease, amend, refer, extend, switch.

cards.f: Why is aciclovir selective for herpes-infected cells?
cards.b: Herpesvirus thymidine kinase activates it, so it accumulates in infected cells, where it stops viral DNA synthesis.
cards.ex: Activation by a viral enzyme confines the drug's action.

cards.f: UK AMR national action plan 2024–2029 human use targets
cards.b: Cut total human antibiotic use 5% from the 2019–20 baseline by 2029; 70% of use from the Access category (UK-AWaRe).
cards.ex: Checked November 2026; Access antibiotics have lower resistance potential.

questions.q: A patient develops spastic paralysis after a contaminated wound. The responsible toxin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters in the spinal cord. Which organism produces it?
questions.why: Tetanus toxin from Clostridium tetani stops inhibitory interneurons releasing their transmitters, so motor neurons fire unchecked and muscles go into spasm. The wound is the portal of entry; the toxin acts far away in the spinal cord.
optWhy: Botulinum toxin also comes from a Clostridium but blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, giving flaccid, not spastic, paralysis.
Correct: tetanus toxin stops inhibitory interneurons releasing glycine and GABA, so motor neurons fire unchecked and muscles go into spasm.
Cholera toxin raises cAMP in gut epithelium and causes watery diarrhoea, not paralysis.
Diphtheria toxin inhibits protein synthesis; it causes local throat damage and toxic effects on heart and nerves, not spasm after a wound.
questions.clue: Spastic paralysis after a contaminated wound; toxin blocks inhibitory transmitter release in the spinal cord.
questions.concept: Exotoxins have specific targets that explain their clinical effects.

followUp.q: A baby develops constipation, poor feeding, a weak cry and floppy limbs. The toxin responsible blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Which organism produces it?
followUp.why: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, so muscles cannot be activated: a descending flaccid weakness. Tetanus toxin gives the opposite picture (spasm) by blocking inhibitory transmitters in the spinal cord. Diphtheria toxin stops protein synthesis. TSST-1 is a superantigen causing toxic shock, not paralysis.

questions.q: Which component of a bacterium is endotoxin?
options: Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane
Peptidoglycan of the Gram-positive cell wall
A protein toxin secreted by Gram-positive bacteria
questions.why: Endotoxin is lipid A, the toxic part of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane. It is released when bacteria die or divide and triggers TLR4, leading to cytokine release, fever and, in large amounts, septic shock.
optWhy: Correct: endotoxin is lipid A, part of the LPS found in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, recognised by TLR4.
Peptidoglycan is a wall polymer in both Gram types; it is recognised by innate receptors but is not what 'endotoxin' means.
A secreted protein toxin is the definition of an exotoxin, the opposite category.
The capsule is a virulence factor that resists phagocytosis, but it is not a toxin.
questions.clue: The word 'endotoxin': a toxin that is part of the bacterium rather than secreted.
questions.concept: Endotoxin (LPS lipid A) versus exotoxins (secreted proteins).

followUp.q: A patient with Escherichia coli in the bloodstream becomes more hypotensive soon after antibiotics start killing large numbers of bacteria. Which host receptor most directly recognises the bacterial molecule released?
followUp.why: Killing Gram-negative bacteria releases LPS, whose lipid A is recognised by TLR4 (with CD14 and MD-2), driving cytokine release. TLR5 recognises flagellin. CD4 is the helper T-cell co-receptor and HIV's receptor. MHC class II presents peptides to CD4 T cells; superantigens, not LPS, bind it.

questions.q: Pus from a skin abscess shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The isolate is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. Which organism is most likely?
questions.why: Gram-positive cocci in clusters suggest staphylococci; a positive catalase test supports this, and a positive coagulase test identifies Staphylococcus aureus, a common cause of abscesses.
optWhy: Streptococci grow in chains and are catalase-negative.
S. epidermidis is a staphylococcus (clusters, catalase-positive) but is coagulase-negative.
Correct: clusters and a positive catalase test indicate a staphylococcus, and coagulase positivity identifies S. aureus.
Neisseria are Gram-negative diplococci, so they would stain pink in pairs.
questions.clue: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase-positive; coagulase-positive.
questions.concept: Using Gram stain, arrangement and bench tests to identify bacteria.

followUp.q: A throat swab from a child with tonsillitis grows Gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative. Which group is most likely?
followUp.why: Gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative are streptococci. Staphylococci form clusters and are catalase-positive. Enterobacteria are Gram-negative rods. Mycobacteria stain poorly with Gram's method and are identified as acid-fast bacilli.

questions.q: Outline the steps of the Gram stain and explain why Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria end up different colours.
markScheme: Crystal violet applied, then iodine (forms a dye complex)
Decolouriser (alcohol or acetone) applied, then red counterstain (e.g. safranin)
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan retains the violet complex, so purple
Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan and outer membrane; violet washed out, counterstain taken up, so pink
questions.modelAnswer: The smear is flooded with crystal violet, then iodine, which forms a large dye–iodine complex in the cells. A decolouriser such as alcohol or acetone is then applied, followed by a red counterstain such as safranin. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that traps the violet complex during decolourising, so they stay purple. Gram-negative bacteria have only a thin peptidoglycan layer beneath an outer membrane; the decolouriser disrupts the outer membrane and the violet complex is washed out, so the cells take up the counterstain and appear pink.
questions.concept: Wall structure determines Gram stain result.

questions.q: Why does influenza A, unlike most other respiratory viruses, periodically cause pandemics through antigenic shift?
options: It integrates into the host genome using integrase
Its genome is segmented, so two strains infecting one cell can swap whole segments
Its RNA polymerase has no proofreading, so it accumulates point mutations
It becomes latent in neurons and reactivates years later
questions.why: Shift needs reassortment: influenza A's genome is split into segments, so co-infection of one cell with two strains (for example human and avian) can produce a virus with a new haemagglutinin or neuraminidase, a subtype to which few people are immune.
optWhy: Error-prone copying is real, but it produces gradual point mutations: antigenic drift, not shift.
Latency in neurons describes herpesviruses.
Integration by integrase describes retroviruses such as HIV.
Correct: reassortment of segments between strains can produce a new haemagglutinin or neuraminidase subtype to which few people are immune.
questions.clue: 'Antigenic shift' and 'pandemics'.
questions.concept: Antigenic shift requires a segmented genome; drift comes from point mutations.

followUp.q: Each year a new seasonal influenza vaccine is produced because circulating strains have accumulated small changes in haemagglutinin. What is this process called?
followUp.why: Small, gradual point mutations in haemagglutinin and neuraminidase are antigenic drift, which is why seasonal vaccines are updated. Shift is a sudden change of subtype by reassortment. Latency describes herpesviruses persisting in nerve ganglia. Reverse transcription is how retroviruses copy RNA into DNA.

questions.q: A patient with advanced HIV develops pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. What kind of organism is this?
questions.why: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus that causes pneumonia when CD4 T-cell counts are very low, as in advanced HIV. It is a classic opportunistic infection of T-cell deficiency.
optWhy: It is a eukaryote, not a prokaryote, so it is not a bacterium.
It was once thought to be a protozoan, which makes this a tempting historical error.
It is a cellular organism, not a virus.
Correct: Pneumocystis jirovecii is classified as a fungus, an opportunist of very low CD4 counts.
questions.clue: Advanced HIV (low CD4 count) and Pneumocystis jirovecii.
questions.concept: Classifying infectious agents and linking opportunists to the immune defect.

followUp.q: A patient on intensive chemotherapy with a very low neutrophil count develops invasive lung infection with a mould that grows as branching hyphae. Which organism is most likely?
followUp.why: Aspergillus is a mould forming branching hyphae and a classic cause of invasive infection in neutropenia. Candida is a yeast (single cells). Pneumocystis is also a fungus, but it is linked mainly with T-cell (CD4) deficiency and does not grow as hyphae. Plasmodium is a protozoan spread by mosquitoes that infects liver and red cells.

questions.q: A patient who had neurosurgery is later diagnosed with Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease. Why is there concern about the reusable surgical instruments even though they were sterilised in the standard way?
options: The agent is a misfolded protein with no nucleic acid that resists standard sterilisation
The agent forms bacterial spores that resist heat
The agent is a fungus protected by ergosterol in its membrane
The agent is an enveloped virus that survives alcohol disinfection
questions.why: CJD is a prion disease. Prions are misfolded forms of the normal prion protein that convert normal PrP and contain no nucleic acid. They resist standard sterilisation, so instruments used in high-risk procedures need special handling.
optWhy: CJD is not caused by a virus, and enveloped viruses are generally more easily inactivated, not less.
Correct: prions are misfolded prion protein with no genome, and standard sterilisation does not reliably destroy them.
Spores are formed by bacteria such as Clostridium and Bacillus; prions are not bacteria.
Ergosterol is a fungal drug target; fungi are destroyed by standard sterilisation and do not cause CJD.
questions.clue: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and instruments sterilised in the standard way.
questions.concept: Prions are infectious proteins that resist standard sterilisation.

followUp.q: Which feature distinguishes prions from viruses?
followUp.why: Prions are proteins with no DNA or RNA; they propagate by converting normal prion protein into the misfolded form. Some viruses, not prions, have envelopes. 70S ribosomes belong to bacteria. Viruses that infect bacteria are bacteriophages; prions affect mammalian nervous tissue.

questions.q: Describe the main stages of a viral replication cycle, using one named virus to illustrate attachment.
markScheme: Attachment of a viral protein to a specific host receptor (named example, e.g. HIV gp120 to CD4 with CCR5/CXCR4, or influenza haemagglutinin to sialic acid)
Entry (fusion or endocytosis) and uncoating of the genome
Replication of the genome and synthesis of viral proteins using host ribosomes
Assembly and release by budding or cell lysis
questions.modelAnswer: A virus first attaches to its target cell: for example, influenza haemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium, which explains why it infects the airway. The virus then enters by membrane fusion or endocytosis and uncoats, releasing its genome. The genome is copied and viral proteins are made on the host's ribosomes; retroviruses such as HIV first reverse-transcribe their RNA into DNA. New capsids and genomes are assembled, and the virions leave by budding through the cell membrane, which gives them an envelope, or by lysing the cell.
questions.concept: Viruses depend on host cells; receptor binding explains tropism.

questions.q: In acute inflammation, which step in neutrophil recruitment depends mainly on selectins?
questions.why: Selectins make weak, rapidly reversible bonds that slow neutrophils so they roll along activated endothelium. Integrins binding ICAM-1 then stop them (firm adhesion), before transmigration and chemotaxis.
optWhy: Correct: selectins make weak, rapidly reversible bonds that slow neutrophils so they roll.
Firm adhesion needs integrins on the neutrophil binding ICAM-1 on the endothelium.
Transmigration is the later squeeze between endothelial cells.
Killing happens after phagocytosis and depends on the respiratory burst and lysosomal enzymes.
questions.clue: 'Depends mainly on selectins'.
questions.concept: Sequence of leucocyte recruitment and the molecule at each step.

followUp.q: Once neutrophils have crossed the vessel wall, which signals guide them towards infected tissue?
followUp.why: IL-8 (a chemokine) and C5a (a complement fragment) are strong neutrophil chemoattractants. IgE and histamine belong to type I hypersensitivity. Perforin and granzymes are how cytotoxic T cells and NK cells kill. Type I interferons put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state.

questions.q: A patient has had three episodes of meningococcal infection. Deficiency of which part of the immune system most likely explains this?
questions.why: The membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) is especially important against Neisseria, so deficiency of terminal complement components classically causes recurrent meningococcal (and gonococcal) infection.
optWhy: IgE defends against helminths and drives allergy; its absence would not single out meningococci.
Correct: Neisseria species are particularly controlled by the membrane attack complex, so C5–C9 deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infection.
NADPH oxidase deficiency (chronic granulomatous disease) causes infections with organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus.
Eosinophils are mainly anti-parasite cells.
questions.clue: Recurrent meningococcal infection.
questions.concept: Specific immune defects produce characteristic infection patterns.

followUp.q: A boy has recurrent Staphylococcus aureus abscesses and an Aspergillus pneumonia. His neutrophils engulf bacteria normally but fail to kill them. Which defect is most likely?
followUp.why: Normal engulfment with failed killing points to absent respiratory burst: chronic granulomatous disease. Terminal complement deficiency gives recurrent Neisseria infection. Absent B cells cause recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria from the second half of the first year, not a killing defect. Mannose-binding lectin starts the lectin complement pathway; it does not explain failed intracellular killing.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student has fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. Blood cultures are taken. CSF results: white cells 1,200 per microlitre, 90% neutrophils (typical normal: under 5); protein 2.1 g/L (typical normal: under 0.4); CSF:plasma glucose ratio 0.2 (typical normal: above 0.66). Values are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory. What is the most likely cause?
options: Normal CSF contaminated by a traumatic tap
questions.why: Bacteria provoke a neutrophil-dominated innate response; neutrophils and bacteria consume glucose, and inflamed, leaky vessels raise CSF protein. Together these give the classical bacterial pattern. Patterns overlap (for example early viral meningitis can be neutrophilic), so results are read with the clinical picture.
optWhy: Viral meningitis typically gives a lymphocyte-predominant rise, mildly raised protein and a normal or slightly low glucose ratio.
Correct: many neutrophils, high protein and a very low glucose ratio are the classical bacterial pattern.
Tuberculous meningitis also lowers glucose and raises protein, but the cells are typically lymphocytes, not 90% neutrophils.
Blood from a traumatic tap adds cells but does not lower the glucose ratio or produce this degree of neutrophilia and protein rise.
questions.clue: 90% neutrophils with a CSF:plasma glucose ratio of 0.2.
questions.concept: Neutrophil versus lymphocyte responses distinguish bacterial from viral infection.

followUp.q: Another patient with headache and neck stiffness has CSF white cells 150 per microlitre, mostly lymphocytes; protein 0.6 g/L; CSF:plasma glucose ratio 0.6 (typical adult UK ranges as before, varying by laboratory). Which is most likely?
options: Bacterial meningitis, because the protein is above normal
Bacterial meningitis, because the glucose ratio is below 0.66
followUp.why: A modest, lymphocyte-predominant rise with mildly raised protein and a normal or slightly low glucose ratio is the classical viral pattern. A mildly raised protein and a slightly low ratio occur in viral meningitis; bacterial meningitis typically gives neutrophils and a very low ratio. 150 cells per microlitre is far above the typical normal of under 5.

questions.q: Explain how the vascular and cellular changes of acute inflammation produce its classic signs.
markScheme: Arteriolar dilation (e.g. histamine, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) increases blood flow: redness and heat
Increased venular permeability lets protein-rich exudate into tissues: swelling
Mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins sensitise nerve endings: pain
Neutrophils are recruited by rolling, adhesion, transmigration and chemotaxis
Swelling and pain cause loss of function
questions.modelAnswer: Mediators such as histamine, prostaglandins and nitric oxide dilate arterioles, so more blood flows through the area, making it red and warm. Venules become leaky, so protein-rich fluid (exudate) escapes into the tissue and it swells. Bradykinin and prostaglandins sensitise pain nerve endings, and the swelling stretches tissue, causing pain.
