Meanwhile neutrophils roll on selectins, adhere through integrins and ICAM-1, migrate between endothelial cells and follow chemotactic signals such as IL-8 and C5a to the site. The combination of pain and swelling leads to loss of function.
questions.concept: Vascular and cellular events explain the cardinal signs.

questions.q: A naive T cell's receptor binds its peptide–MHC complex on a cell that provides no co-stimulation. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The T cell divides and becomes an effector cell
The T cell switches antibody class to IgG
The T cell is destroyed by the membrane attack complex
questions.why: A naive T cell needs signal 1 (TCR binding peptide–MHC) and signal 2 (co-stimulation, mainly CD28 binding CD80/CD86) to activate. Signal 1 alone tends to cause anergy, which helps prevent responses to self-antigens on ordinary tissue cells that lack co-stimulatory molecules.
optWhy: Correct: signal 1 without signal 2 tends to switch the cell off, which supports tolerance to self.
Clonal expansion into effector cells needs co-stimulation (signal 2) and cytokines (signal 3) as well as signal 1.
Class switching is something B cells do, with T-cell help; T cells do not make antibody.
Complement does not destroy T cells for lacking co-stimulation.
questions.clue: 'No co-stimulation'.
questions.concept: Two-signal activation of naive T cells.

followUp.q: Which interaction provides the main co-stimulatory signal (signal 2) to a naive T cell?
options: CD40 ligand on the T cell binding CD40 on a B cell
CD28 on the T cell binding CD80/CD86 on the dendritic cell
followUp.why: CD28 binding CD80/CD86 (B7) on an activated dendritic cell is the classic signal 2. CD40 ligand–CD40 is how helper T cells help B cells (for example class switching). CD4 binds MHC class II, not class I. TLR4 sensing LPS helps activate dendritic cells (which then express B7), but it is not itself the T-cell co-stimulatory signal.

questions.q: A virus-infected epithelial cell is killed by a cytotoxic T cell. Which molecule on the infected cell presented the viral peptide?
questions.why: Viral proteins made inside the cell are processed and displayed on MHC class I, which almost all nucleated cells express. CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognise this complex and kill the cell with perforin and granzymes.
optWhy: MHC class II presents engulfed material to CD4 helper T cells and is found on professional antigen-presenting cells, not ordinary epithelium.
CD4 is a co-receptor on helper T cells, not a presenting molecule.
Correct: viral proteins made inside the cell are shown on MHC class I, which almost all nucleated cells express and CD8 T cells recognise.
CD28 is the co-stimulatory receptor on T cells.
questions.clue: Virus-infected epithelial cell; cytotoxic T cell.
questions.concept: MHC class I presents intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells.

followUp.q: A dendritic cell in a lymph node presents peptides from engulfed bacteria to activate a naive helper T cell. Which pairing is correct?
followUp.why: Engulfed (extracellular) material is presented on MHC class II to CD4 helper T cells. CD4 binds class II and CD8 binds class I, so the mixed pairings are wrong. MHC class I with CD8 is the route for intracellular proteins such as viral antigens, not engulfed bacteria presented to helper cells.

questions.q: Blood tests show high levels of specific IgM, with little specific IgG, against a virus. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Infection years ago with lasting immunity
Immunity from a vaccine given in childhood
questions.why: IgM is made first in a primary response, so a high specific IgM with little IgG points to a recent first infection. As the response matures, class switching produces IgG, which persists.
optWhy: Past infection with lasting immunity would show mainly IgG, because the IgM response fades.
Maternal antibody that crosses the placenta is IgG, not IgM.
Childhood vaccination leaves IgG and memory cells, not a high IgM years later.
Correct: IgM is made first in a primary response, so high IgM with little IgG points to a recent first infection.
questions.clue: High specific IgM, little specific IgG.
questions.concept: Antibody class reveals the timing of infection.

followUp.q: A newborn's blood contains IgG against rubella but no rubella IgM. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Congenital rubella infection acquired in the womb
Maternal IgG that crossed the placenta
The baby's own secondary immune response
Antibody from breast milk absorbed from the gut
followUp.why: IgG crosses the placenta, so a newborn carries the mother's IgG. A baby infected in the womb would make its own IgM, which does not come from the mother because IgM does not cross the placenta. A newborn has had no earlier exposure, so cannot mount a secondary response. Breast-milk antibody is mainly IgA, which protects the gut surface rather than entering the blood.

questions.q: Describe how a T-dependent B-cell response produces high-affinity IgG antibodies.
markScheme: B cell binds antigen via its B-cell receptor, internalises it and presents peptide on MHC class II
Helper T cell (activated earlier by a dendritic cell) recognises the same antigen and provides help via CD40L–CD40 and cytokines
In the germinal centre, class switching changes IgM to IgG
Somatic hypermutation plus selection for best binding gives affinity maturation
B cells become plasma cells (secrete antibody) and memory B cells
questions.modelAnswer: A naive B cell binds antigen through its B-cell receptor, takes it in and displays peptides from it on MHC class II. A CD4 helper T cell that was activated by a dendritic cell presenting the same antigen recognises this complex and helps the B cell: CD40 ligand on the T cell binds CD40 on the B cell, and cytokines are released. Some activated B cells enter germinal centres in lymph nodes. There, class switching changes the antibody from IgM to IgG (or IgA or IgE) while keeping the same specificity, and somatic hypermutation alters the antigen-binding region; B cells with the best-binding receptors are selected to survive, so affinity rises. The selected cells become plasma cells that secrete high-affinity IgG, or long-lived memory B cells.
questions.concept: T-cell help drives class switching and affinity maturation.

questions.q: Why are plain polysaccharide vaccines poorly effective in children under about two years old?
options: Polysaccharides are destroyed by stomach acid
Polysaccharides are T-independent antigens, and infants make weak T-independent antibody responses with little memory
Maternal IgA in breast milk neutralises the vaccine
Infants lack MHC class I molecules
questions.why: Polysaccharides cannot be processed and presented on MHC class II, so they activate B cells without T-cell help. Young children make weak T-independent responses with little class switching or memory; conjugating the polysaccharide to a protein fixes this.
optWhy: Breast-milk IgA protects the infant's gut and does not neutralise an injected vaccine.
Infants do express MHC class I, and class I is not the issue for antibody responses to polysaccharide.
These vaccines are injected, not swallowed, so stomach acid is irrelevant.
Correct: polysaccharides cannot be presented to helper T cells, so they trigger only T-independent responses, weak in young children and with little memory.
questions.clue: 'Plain polysaccharide' and 'under about two years'.
questions.concept: T-independent antigens give weak responses in infants; conjugation recruits T-cell help.

followUp.q: Which feature of conjugate vaccines explains why they generate memory in infants?
options: The polysaccharide is presented on MHC class I to CD8 T cells
The vaccine contains live bacteria that replicate briefly
Carrier-protein peptides are presented on MHC class II to helper T cells, which then help polysaccharide-specific B cells
The adjuvant replaces the need for T-cell help
followUp.why: A B cell that recognises the polysaccharide takes up the whole conjugate and presents peptides from the carrier protein on MHC class II; helper T cells recognising those peptides give it CD40 ligand and cytokine help, so it class-switches and forms memory. Polysaccharides are not presented on MHC class I. Conjugate vaccines are not live. Adjuvants boost innate signals but do not substitute for T-cell help.

questions.q: A woman develops an itchy rash where a nickel watch strap touched her skin, appearing about two days after contact. Which type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.why: Contact dermatitis to nickel is delayed, T-cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity: sensitised T cells release cytokines at the contact site, so the reaction peaks one to three days after exposure.
optWhy: Type I is IgE-mediated and appears within minutes, so the two-day delay rules it out.
Correct: contact dermatitis to nickel is delayed, T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity, appearing one to three days after exposure.
Type II involves antibodies against cell-surface or tissue antigens, as in transfusion reactions.
Type III involves immune complex deposition, as in serum sickness, not a reaction confined to the contact site.
questions.clue: Rash at the contact site appearing about two days later.
questions.concept: Gell and Coombs classification by mechanism and timing.

followUp.q: Minutes after a wasp sting, a man develops widespread urticaria, wheeze and low blood pressure. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: IgE cross-linked on mast cells, releasing histamine (type I)
Immune complexes deposited in vessel walls (type III)
Sensitised T cells releasing cytokines (type IV)
IgG against red cell antigens (type II)
followUp.why: A reaction within minutes, with urticaria, wheeze and hypotension, is anaphylaxis: allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, which release histamine and other mediators. Immune complex disease develops over days; type IV peaks after one to three days; antibody against red cells causes haemolysis, not this picture.

questions.q: A 9-month-old boy has had two pneumonias and recurrent ear infections with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae since about 6 months of age. All immunoglobulin classes are very low and there are almost no B cells in his blood; T-cell numbers are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.why: Recurrent infection with encapsulated bacteria beginning in the second half of the first year, absent B cells and very low immunoglobulins fit X-linked agammaglobulinaemia. Maternal IgG protected him for the first months.
optWhy: Correct: a BTK mutation stops B-cell maturation, so antibody is absent and encapsulated bacteria cause infections once maternal IgG wanes.
DiGeorge syndrome reduces T cells (small or absent thymus), giving viral and fungal infections; B cells are present.
Chronic granulomatous disease is a phagocyte killing defect with normal antibody levels, typically Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus.
Terminal complement deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infection, with normal B cells and antibody.
questions.clue: Onset about 6 months; encapsulated bacteria; almost no B cells, normal T cells.
questions.concept: Working from the infection pattern back to the missing immune component.

followUp.q: A baby with a 22q11.2 deletion, a heart defect and low blood calcium has recurrent viral and fungal infections. Which component is most likely deficient?
options: B cells, because of a BTK mutation
T cells, because the thymus is small or absent
followUp.why: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) affects development of the thymus (and parathyroids and heart), so T-cell output falls and viral and fungal infections follow. BTK mutation causes absent B cells and bacterial infections. NADPH oxidase defects cause bacterial and fungal infections with normal T cells. Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to Neisseria.

questions.q: Compare live attenuated and inactivated vaccines, giving one example of each and one safety consideration.
markScheme: Live attenuated: weakened organism replicates, strong long-lasting antibody and T-cell response, often fewer doses (example: MMR(V) or BCG)
Inactivated or subunit/toxoid: cannot replicate, weaker response, usually needs adjuvant and boosters (example: inactivated polio, tetanus toxoid)
Safety: live vaccines generally avoided in significant immunosuppression and in pregnancy
Inactivated vaccines cannot cause the infection and can be used in immunosuppressed people (though the response may be weaker)
questions.modelAnswer: Live attenuated vaccines, such as MMRV, contain weakened organisms that replicate briefly, mimicking natural infection; they give strong, long-lasting antibody and T-cell responses, often from fewer doses. Inactivated vaccines, such as inactivated polio vaccine, or toxoids such as tetanus, cannot replicate, so they give weaker responses and usually need adjuvants and booster doses. The key safety point is that live vaccines can cause disease in people with significant immunosuppression and are generally avoided in them and in pregnancy, whereas inactivated vaccines cannot cause the infection and can be given to immunosuppressed people, although their response may be weaker.
questions.concept: Replication gives live vaccines both their strength and their risk.

questions.q: Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 in England, when must a registered medical practitioner notify a case of a notifiable disease?
options: On suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation
Only if the patient is admitted to hospital
Only once the laboratory confirms the organism
questions.why: The regulations require notification on reasonable grounds for suspicion, so that public-health action is not delayed. UKHSA asks for urgent cases to be phoned to the health protection team within 24 hours and all cases to be reported online within 3 days (checked November 2026).
optWhy: Waiting for confirmation would delay public-health action such as contact tracing; the regulations do not require it.
Correct: the duty is triggered by reasonable grounds for suspicion; laboratories notify causative agents separately.
Statutory notification is a legal duty and does not depend on consent.
Notification applies in any setting, including general practice.
questions.clue: 'When must ... notify'.
questions.concept: The notification duty is triggered by clinical suspicion.

followUp.q: A GP strongly suspects meningococcal septicaemia in a child and arranges emergency admission. What does UKHSA guidance say about notification?
options: Report through the online service within 3 days only, as it is a routine notification
Leave notification to the hospital laboratory once cultures are positive
Notify only if a second linked case appears
Phone the local health protection team urgently (within 24 hours) and also report through the online service within 3 days
followUp.why: Meningococcal septicaemia is listed as an urgent notifiable disease, so the doctor who suspects it phones the health protection team within 24 hours (contacts may need antibiotics or vaccine) and also completes the written/online report within 3 days. It is not a routine notification. Laboratory notification of the organism is a separate duty and does not replace the clinician's. One case is enough to notify.

questions.q: A disease has R0 = 10. A vaccine is 95% effective. What is the herd immunity threshold (the proportion of the population that must be immune)?
questions.why: The threshold is 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/10 = 0.9, so 90% must be immune. Vaccine effectiveness matters for the coverage target (0.9 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 94.7%), not for the threshold itself.
optWhy: 10% is 1/R0, the proportion that can remain susceptible, not the proportion that must be immune.
Correct: H = 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/10 = 0.9; vaccine effectiveness does not change the threshold itself.
85.5% multiplies 0.9 by 0.95 instead of dividing, which is wrong for both quantities.
94.7% is 0.9 ÷ 0.95: the vaccine coverage needed to reach the threshold, which answers a different question.
questions.clue: The question asks for the proportion that must be immune, not the coverage.
questions.concept: Herd immunity threshold H = 1 − 1/R0; coverage = H ÷ effectiveness.

followUp.q: Measles has an R0 of about 15 in a population, and a vaccine is 95% effective. Roughly what vaccine coverage is needed to reach the herd immunity threshold (simple model)?
followUp.why: H = 1 − 1/15 ≈ 0.933; coverage = 0.933 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 0.982, about 98%. About 93% is the threshold itself, ignoring vaccine failure. About 89% multiplies by 0.95 instead of dividing. About 7% is 1/R0, the proportion that may remain susceptible.

questions.q: An infection has R0 = 4. In a town, 60% of people are immune. Using the simple model, what is the effective reproduction number?
questions.why: Effective R ≈ R0 × proportion susceptible = 4 × (1 − 0.6) = 4 × 0.4 = 1.6. Because R is above 1, the epidemic would still grow; the threshold here would be 1 − 1/4 = 75% immune.
optWhy: Correct: R ≈ R0 × proportion susceptible = 4 × 0.4 = 1.6, so cases would still increase.
2.4 multiplies by the proportion immune (0.6) instead of the proportion susceptible.
3.4 subtracts 0.6 from R0, mixing a proportion with a number of cases.
6.7 divides R0 by 0.6, which would make immunity increase spread.
questions.clue: R0 = 4 with 60% immune (so 40% susceptible).
questions.concept: Effective R ≈ R0 × proportion susceptible.

followUp.q: A measles-like infection has R0 = 12, and 85% of a school community is immune. Using the simple model, what is the effective reproduction number?
followUp.why: R ≈ 12 × (1 − 0.85) = 12 × 0.15 = 1.8, so an outbreak could still grow despite 85% immunity. 10.2 multiplies by the proportion immune. 11.15 subtracts 0.85 from 12. 14.1 divides 12 by 0.85.

questions.q: A cluster of diarrhoea and vomiting follows a wedding meal. Outline how the outbreak would be investigated and controlled.
markScheme: Confirm the outbreak and diagnosis (clinical details, stool samples)
Write a case definition and find cases (guest list, questionnaires)
Plot an epidemic curve: a single sharp peak suggests a point source such as one meal
Compare food histories of ill and well guests to identify the likely vehicle
Control: remove the source, hygiene advice (soap and water for norovirus), exclude ill food handlers, notify/inform the health protection team
questions.modelAnswer: First confirm that there really is an outbreak and establish the likely diagnosis, collecting clinical details and stool samples. Write a case definition (who counts as a case, when and where), then actively find cases, for example by contacting everyone on the guest list. Plot an epidemic curve: a single sharp peak about one incubation period after the meal suggests a point source. Compare what ill and well guests ate to find the food most strongly associated with illness. Control measures are to withdraw the suspected food, investigate the kitchen, exclude ill food handlers until they are no longer infectious, give hygiene advice (soap and water, since alcohol rub is less reliable against norovirus) and work with the local UKHSA health protection team, notifying suspected food poisoning as required.
questions.concept: Outbreak investigation: case definition, epidemic curve, source and control.

questions.q: Why might a patient in a single room under contact precautions for MRSA be at risk of poorer care, according to research on isolation?
options: Isolated patients are legally barred from visitors
Studies have linked isolation with fewer clinician contacts and more anxiety and depression
Contact precautions require stopping all antibiotics
Isolation rooms increase transmission of MRSA to the patient
questions.why: A 2020 systematic review of mainly observational studies found isolated patients had higher depression and anxiety scores, fewer contacts from healthcare workers and more adverse events such as falls and pressure ulcers. Causation cannot be proven, but staff should make deliberate efforts to check on isolated patients.
optWhy: Isolation aims to reduce MRSA transmission, not increase it.
There is no legal ban on visitors; visitors are usually allowed with precautions.
Correct: mainly observational studies associate isolation with more anxiety and depression, less clinician contact and more adverse events.
Contact precautions concern hand hygiene, gloves and aprons, not stopping antibiotics.
questions.clue: 'According to research on isolation'.
questions.concept: Infection-control isolation has psychological and safety costs.

followUp.q: A nurse notices that a patient in a side room with C. difficile has become withdrawn and has had a fall. What is the most appropriate response, based on evidence about isolation?
options: Plan regular, deliberate contact and check mood, orientation and falls risk while keeping the precautions
End isolation early because its harms outweigh the infection risk
Avoid entering the room so as to reduce transmission
Assume the fall is unrelated to isolation
followUp.why: The precautions are still needed to protect others, so the answer is to counter the known harms: planned contact, attention to mood and delirium, and falls prevention. Ending precautions early ignores transmission risk. Avoiding the room worsens the reduced contact that research links with harm. Falls are among the adverse events reported more often in isolated patients.

questions.q: A man newly diagnosed with HIV says he will not start treatment because he fears his workmates will find out. Which concept best explains the barrier he describes?
questions.why: He fears being labelled and discriminated against if his diagnosis becomes known: anticipated stigma. Addressing it (confidentiality, accurate information such as U=U, peer support) can make treatment possible.
optWhy: The sick role describes the rights and duties society gives a sick person; if anything it would push him to accept treatment.
Antigenic drift is a viral mechanism of gradual mutation, unrelated to behaviour.
The inverse care law is a population pattern (good care least available where most needed), not this man's personal fear.
Correct: he fears being labelled and discriminated against if the diagnosis becomes known, a recognised reason for delayed or refused HIV care.
questions.clue: 'Fears his workmates will find out'.
questions.concept: Stigma delays testing and treatment.

followUp.q: A young man with symptoms of a sexually transmitted infection delays seeking help because he is afraid staff at his GP practice will judge him. Which response best addresses this barrier?
options: Tell him all sexually transmitted infections are notifiable, so he must attend
Offer confidential, non-judgemental care (for example a sexual health clinic) and explain how confidentiality works
Advise him to wait and see whether the symptoms settle
Explain that the sick role obliges him to seek help
followUp.why: The barrier is anticipated stigma, so the effective response reduces the fear: confidential, non-judgemental services and clear information about confidentiality. Most sexually transmitted infections are not on the notifiable diseases list, and pressure tends to deter people. Waiting delays treatment and allows onward transmission. Quoting the sick role does nothing to address his fear of judgement.

questions.q: A parent says she will not bring her toddler for the MMRV vaccine because measles 'doesn't really happen any more'. Which factor in the WHO SAGE model of vaccine hesitancy does this mainly reflect?
questions.why: She doubts the need for vaccination because the disease seems rare: complacency. A helpful response explains that measles is still circulating, that it is highly infectious, and that it stays rare only while coverage is high.
optWhy: Confidence concerns trust in vaccine safety, effectiveness or the system delivering it; she has not questioned these.
Convenience concerns access, such as appointment times or travel.
Anticipated stigma is fear of being judged; it is not part of the SAGE three Cs.
Correct: complacency means low perceived risk of the disease, so vaccination seems unnecessary.
questions.clue: 'Doesn't really happen any more'.
questions.concept: Confidence, complacency and convenience need different responses.

followUp.q: A father wants his child vaccinated but keeps missing appointments because clinic times clash with his shifts. Which factor is this, and what is most likely to help?
options: Confidence: give information about vaccine safety
Complacency: explain the risks of the disease
Convenience: offer flexible or out-of-hours appointments
followUp.why: He already intends to vaccinate, so the barrier is access (convenience), best met by flexible appointments. Safety information addresses confidence, which he has not questioned. Explaining disease risk addresses complacency, which he does not show. Confidentiality reassurance addresses stigma, which is not the issue here.

questions.q: A student is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Describe four social or psychological effects this diagnosis might have on her.
markScheme: Stigma or fear of stigma (TB's history; fear of being seen as dirty or contagious)
Anxiety about infecting family or housemates, and the disruption of contact tracing
Social isolation during the infectious period (time off study or work, loneliness)
Financial or academic disruption, and the burden of a long treatment course affecting mood and adherence
questions.modelAnswer: She may feel stigmatised, or fear that others will see her as dirty or dangerous because of TB's history, which can make her reluctant to tell friends. She may be anxious that she has infected housemates or family, and find contact tracing embarrassing. During the infectious period she may need to stay away from university, causing isolation and loneliness. The long treatment course can disrupt study, work and income, and the strain may cause low mood, which in turn can affect adherence. Addressing these openly and offering support helps her complete treatment.
questions.concept: Infection has social and psychological consequences that affect outcomes.

questions.q: A Staphylococcus aureus isolate is resistant to flucloxacillin and other β-lactams because it carries the mecA gene. What does this gene do?
options: Encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for β-lactams
Encodes an efflux pump that removes the drug
Removes porins so the drug cannot enter
Encodes a β-lactamase that hydrolyses the drug
questions.why: mecA encodes PBP2a, a transpeptidase that β-lactams bind poorly, so cell-wall synthesis continues in their presence. This altered target, not an enzyme, is what makes MRSA resistant to flucloxacillin.
optWhy: β-lactamase production is a different, common mechanism, but flucloxacillin is designed to resist staphylococcal penicillinase.
Correct: PBP2a keeps building the cell wall because β-lactams bind it poorly; this target change defines MRSA.
Efflux pumps matter for other resistance but are not what mecA encodes.
Porin loss limits entry through the Gram-negative outer membrane; S. aureus is Gram-positive and has no outer membrane.
questions.clue: mecA and resistance to flucloxacillin.
questions.concept: Altered target as a resistance mechanism.

followUp.q: An Escherichia coli isolate resists many cephalosporins because it produces a plasmid-encoded enzyme that hydrolyses the β-lactam ring. Which mechanism is this?
options: Enzymatic inactivation by an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)
Loss of peptidoglycan from the cell wall
followUp.why: An enzyme that hydrolyses the β-lactam ring and inactivates many cephalosporins is an extended-spectrum β-lactamase, often carried on plasmids with other resistance genes. PBP2a is MRSA's altered target. Efflux pumps remove intact drug rather than destroying it. Loss of peptidoglycan is not how E. coli resists cephalosporins; the stem describes an enzyme that destroys the drug.

questions.q: Broth tubes containing an antibiotic at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 mg/L are inoculated with a bacterium. After incubation, the 0.25, 0.5 and 1 mg/L tubes are cloudy and the others are clear. What is the MIC?
questions.why: The MIC is the lowest concentration with no visible growth: the first clear tube, 2 mg/L. The result is then compared with the drug's breakpoints to classify the organism as susceptible or resistant.
optWhy: Correct: the MIC is the lowest concentration with no visible growth, the first clear tube.
1 mg/L is the highest concentration that still allowed growth, a common off-by-one-tube slip.
8 mg/L is the highest concentration tested; it inhibits growth but is not the minimum.
0.25 mg/L is the lowest concentration tested, and it did not inhibit growth.
questions.clue: Cloudy up to 1 mg/L, clear from 2 mg/L.
questions.concept: MIC = lowest concentration preventing visible growth.

followUp.q: In a dilution series of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 mg/L, tubes up to and including 4 mg/L are cloudy and tubes from 8 mg/L upwards are clear. What is the MIC?
followUp.why: The first clear tube is 8 mg/L, the lowest concentration preventing visible growth. 4 mg/L still allowed growth. 32 mg/L is the highest concentration tested, not the minimum. 1 mg/L is the lowest tested and was cloudy.

questions.q: A 64-year-old man was started promptly on a broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic for suspected pneumonia with sepsis. At 48 hours he is afebrile and eating, and blood cultures have grown an organism sensitive to a narrow-spectrum agent. Which Start smart then focus decision is most appropriate?
options: Refer for outpatient intravenous therapy on the same broad-spectrum drug
Extend the broad-spectrum drug for the full course to be safe
Amend to a narrower-spectrum agent, with a documented stop or review date
Cease all antibiotics because he is afebrile
questions.why: UKHSA's toolkit asks for a documented review at 48–72 hours with one of five outcomes: cease, amend, refer, extend or switch. With a confirmed, sensitive organism and clinical improvement, amending to a narrower agent (and switching to oral when criteria are met) is the stewardship choice (checked November 2026).
optWhy: Continuing a broad-spectrum drug without need adds C. difficile risk and selection pressure; extension should be justified and dated.
Correct: a known, sensitive organism allows the spectrum to be narrowed, reducing harm to normal flora and selection for resistance.
Pneumonia with bacteraemia still needs treatment; improvement does not mean infection has gone.
Referral for outpatient therapy suits some patients, but keeping an unnecessarily broad drug ignores the culture result.
questions.clue: Improving at 48 hours with a culture showing sensitivity to a narrow-spectrum agent.
questions.concept: Start smart then focus: review at 48–72 hours and narrow where possible.

followUp.q: A woman started on antibiotics for suspected urinary infection is reviewed at 48 hours: the urine culture is negative and her symptoms are now explained by another diagnosis. Which decision fits Start smart then focus?
followUp.why: With no evidence of infection, the antibiotic should be stopped (cease). Amending or switching assumes infection still needs treating; extending prolongs unnecessary exposure, adding side-effects, C. difficile risk and selection for resistance.

questions.q: Using named drug classes, explain how antibacterial drugs achieve selective toxicity. (Do not give doses.)
markScheme: Principle: target present in bacteria but absent or different in humans
Cell wall: β-lactams block peptidoglycan cross-linking (humans have no peptidoglycan)
Ribosome: aminoglycosides/tetracyclines (30S) or macrolides (50S) target 70S bacterial ribosomes, not human 80S
Nucleic acid: fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV
Folate: sulfonamides and trimethoprim block bacterial folate synthesis; humans take in folate from diet
questions.modelAnswer: Selective toxicity means hitting a target that bacteria have and human cells lack, or that differs enough to be hit selectively. β-lactams such as penicillins block the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, which human cells do not have. Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and macrolides the 50S subunit of the bacterial 70S ribosome, sparing our 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes. Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Sulfonamides and trimethoprim block steps in folate synthesis; bacteria must make their own folate, whereas we absorb it from food, and trimethoprim binds bacterial dihydrofolate reductase far more strongly than the human enzyme.
questions.concept: Selective toxicity exploits differences between bacterial and human cells.

questions.q: A previously healthy 30-year-old develops pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Describe how the innate and adaptive immune systems respond to this infection, and explain why a conjugate vaccine protects infants against pneumococcal disease when a plain polysaccharide vaccine does not.
markScheme: Barriers breached; organism is a Gram-positive encapsulated coccus; capsule resists phagocytosis
Innate recognition by PRRs (e.g. TLRs) on alveolar macrophages; cytokines IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6; fever and CRP
Complement activation (alternative/lectin, later classical) with C3b opsonisation and C5a recruitment of neutrophils; neutrophil recruitment steps
Dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes; CD4 T-cell activation (signals 1–3); Th17/neutrophil help
B-cell response: IgM then class-switched IgG via T-cell help; anti-capsule antibody opsonises, enabling phagocytosis; memory
Plain polysaccharide is T-independent: weak in under-twos, little memory
Conjugate links polysaccharide to protein: helper T cells recruited, class switching, affinity maturation and memory in infants
Clear structure, correct terminology, links between innate and adaptive arms
questions.modelAnswer:
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive coccus with a polysaccharide capsule. When it reaches the alveoli, the capsule is its main defence, because it hinders complement deposition and phagocytosis.

Innate response. Alveolar macrophages recognise pneumococcal components through pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors. They release IL-1, TNF-α and IL-6, which cause fever by raising the hypothalamic set point and, through IL-6, make the liver produce C-reactive protein, which can itself bind pneumococcal cell wall components and activate complement. Complement is activated by the alternative and lectin pathways, and later by the classical pathway once antibody appears. C3b coats the bacteria (opsonisation), and C5a attracts neutrophils. Endothelium in the lung becomes activated: neutrophils roll on selectins, adhere through integrins binding ICAM-1, migrate into the alveoli and follow chemotactic gradients. Leaky vessels and the influx of neutrophils fill the alveoli with exudate, producing consolidation. Neutrophils ingest opsonised bacteria and kill them using the respiratory burst and lysosomal enzymes.

Adaptive response. Dendritic cells take up bacterial antigens and migrate to lymph nodes, presenting peptides on MHC class II to naive CD4 T cells with co-stimulation (CD80/86 to CD28) and cytokines. Helper T cells, including Th17 cells that promote neutrophil recruitment, expand. B cells that recognise pneumococcal antigens make IgM first. With T-cell help through CD40 ligand and cytokines, B cells in germinal centres class-switch to IgG and undergo affinity maturation. Anti-capsular IgG is especially protective: it opsonises the bacteria through Fc receptors and activates complement, overcoming the capsule's defence. Memory B and T cells give faster protection on re-exposure to the same serotype.

Vaccines in infants. A plain polysaccharide vaccine is a T-independent antigen: polysaccharide cannot be processed and presented on MHC class II, so it activates B cells by cross-linking their receptors without T-cell help. Children under about two years make weak T-independent responses, and such responses produce little class switching or memory. A conjugate vaccine links capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein. B cells specific for the polysaccharide take up the conjugate and present peptides from the carrier protein to helper T cells. This converts the response into a T-dependent one, giving class-switched, high-affinity IgG against the capsule and immunological memory, even in infants. This is why a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is part of the UK infant schedule.
questions.concept: Innate and adaptive responses to an encapsulated bacterium; conjugate vaccines recruit T-cell help.

questions.q: Antimicrobial resistance has been called a major threat to modern medicine. Explain how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics and how resistance spreads, and discuss how antimicrobial stewardship in the UK aims to limit it. (Do not give doses.)
markScheme: Distinguishes intrinsic vs acquired resistance
Acquisition by mutation and horizontal gene transfer (conjugation, transformation, transduction); plasmids may carry several resistance genes
Mechanisms with examples: enzymatic inactivation (β-lactamases, ESBLs, carbapenemases), altered target (mecA/PBP2a, VRE), reduced permeability (porins), efflux
Selection pressure: any antimicrobial use, especially broad-spectrum and unnecessary use; spread between people, in healthcare and via animals/environment (One Health)
Stewardship principles: right drug, right time, right duration; narrowest effective spectrum; cultures before treatment; review
UK specifics: NICE NG15; UKHSA Start smart then focus with 48–72 h review (cease, amend, refer, extend, switch); national action plan 2024–2029 targets
Infection prevention and vaccination reduce the need for antibiotics
Balanced discussion, e.g. tension between treating sepsis promptly and avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum use
questions.modelAnswer:
Resistance can be intrinsic or acquired. Intrinsic resistance is a natural property of a species: vancomycin cannot cross the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, and aminoglycosides are not taken up by anaerobes. Acquired resistance arises when a previously susceptible organism changes.

Bacteria acquire resistance by mutation or by gaining genes from other bacteria. Because bacteria divide rapidly, rare mutations (for example in DNA gyrase, giving fluoroquinolone resistance) appear in large populations. Horizontal gene transfer is often more important: conjugation passes plasmids through a pilus, transformation takes up free DNA and transduction uses bacteriophages. Plasmids can carry several resistance genes together, so one transfer may confer multidrug resistance.

The resistance genes act through a few mechanisms. Enzymes may destroy the drug: β-lactamases, extended-spectrum β-lactamases that inactivate many cephalosporins, and carbapenemases. The target may change: MRSA carries mecA, encoding PBP2a, which β-lactams bind poorly, and vancomycin-resistant enterococci alter the D-Ala-D-Ala target. Entry may be reduced by losing porins, or the drug may be pumped out by efflux pumps.

Resistance spreads because every use of an antimicrobial kills susceptible organisms and leaves resistant ones, including among normal flora. Broad-spectrum and unnecessary use, such as antibiotics for viral infections, adds selection pressure. Resistant organisms then spread between patients through hands and the environment in hospitals, in the community and between people, animals and the environment, which is why a One Health approach is advocated.

Stewardship aims to keep antimicrobials effective while still treating infection promptly. NICE guideline NG15 (2015) sets out organisational systems for it. UKHSA's Start smart then focus toolkit, updated in 2023, asks prescribers to start antibiotics only with clear evidence of infection, to take cultures first where possible without delaying treatment of severe sepsis, to follow local guidelines and to document the indication and a duration or review date. At 48 to 72 hours the prescription is reviewed and the decision recorded: cease, amend (usually to a narrower drug), refer to outpatient or virtual-ward care, extend with a stop date, or switch from intravenous to oral. The UK national action plan for 2024 to 2029 sets targets including a 5% reduction in total human antibiotic use from the 2019 to 2020 baseline by 2029 and 70% of use from the Access category of the UK-adapted AWaRe classification, the antibiotics with lower resistance potential.

Prevention also reduces demand for antibiotics: hand hygiene and other infection control, vaccination (for example against pneumococcus and influenza), and clean water and sanitation.

There are tensions. A septic patient needs prompt broad treatment, and withholding it costs lives; NICE's sepsis guideline for adults (NG253, 2025) asks for antibiotics within an hour for those at high risk. But continuing broad-spectrum drugs without review fuels resistance and C. difficile. Stewardship resolves this by treating promptly and then reviewing and narrowing, rather than by withholding treatment.
questions.concept: Resistance mechanisms, spread and UK stewardship.

cases.title: Fever, cough and a high NEWS2

steps.text: A 71-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter. She has had three days of cough with green sputum and since this morning has seemed muddled. Observations: respiratory rate 28/min, SpO₂ 92% on air, heart rate 122/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, temperature 38.9 °C; she is newly confused. Crackles and bronchial breathing are heard at the right lung base. She has no urinary symptoms, rash, headache or neck stiffness.

ask.q: What is the most likely source of infection?
ask.why: A productive cough with focal signs at one lung base (crackles, bronchial breathing) points to pneumonia. New confusion here is most likely a sign of sepsis rather than meningitis: there is no headache, neck stiffness or rash. She has no urinary symptoms, although NICE still suggests considering urine analysis in suspected sepsis. No wound or skin change is described.

steps.text: The nurse calculates a NEWS2 score of 13: she scores on every parameter except supplemental oxygen, and new confusion alone scores 3.

ask.q: Under NICE NG253 (checked November 2026), what does this mean for her care?
options: Moderate risk: antibiotics can be deferred for up to 3 hours while more information is gathered
Low risk: repeat observations in 4 to 6 hours
Wait for the CRP result to confirm whether she has sepsis before giving antibiotics
High risk (NEWS2 7 or more): urgent assessment, blood cultures and lactate, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating NEWS2
ask.why: In acute hospitals NG253 uses NEWS2 to stratify risk: 7 or more is high risk, needing urgent assessment and antibiotics within 1 hour. At moderate risk (5–6) antibiotics are due within 3 hours and can be deferred while more information is gathered; at low risk (1–4), within 6 hours. CRP neither defines sepsis nor should delay treatment; it also lags behind the illness.

steps.text: The team prepares to give the first antibiotic dose within the hour.

ask.q: Which approach to samples best fits sepsis care and antimicrobial stewardship?
options: Take blood cultures and other relevant samples (sputum, blood gas with lactate, FBC, CRP, kidney function) and arrange a chest X-ray, without letting this delay the antibiotics
Give antibiotics first and take blood cultures after 48 hours to see whether treatment is working
Take no samples, because she clearly needs antibiotics whatever the results
Hold antibiotics until the chest X-ray and all blood results are back
ask.why: Samples taken before the first dose give the best chance of identifying the organism, which later allows the drug to be narrowed (Start smart then focus). Cultures taken after antibiotics have a lower yield. Skipping samples removes the information needed for review. Waiting for every result breaches the 1-hour target for high-risk patients.

steps.text: Results: white cell count 19.6 ×10⁹/L (neutrophils 17.2 ×10⁹/L), CRP 240 mg/L, venous lactate 3.4 mmol/L. The chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.

ask.q: What best explains her raised lactate and low blood pressure?
options: An IgE-mediated (type I) allergic reaction to the bacteria
Lactate produced by bacteria in the consolidated lung
A dysregulated host response: cytokines dilate blood vessels and make them leaky, reducing tissue perfusion
Fever-related dehydration alone, without any effect on vessels
ask.why: IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6 and other mediators, released in excess, cause vasodilation and capillary leak, so blood pressure and tissue perfusion fall and cells shift towards anaerobic metabolism, raising lactate. This is why Sepsis-3 describes sepsis as organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response. It is not an IgE-mediated reaction. Bacterial lactate production does not explain the circulatory changes. Fluid loss can contribute, but it does not account for organ dysfunction on its own.

steps.text: Outcome: at 48 hours she is more alert and eating. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to a narrow-spectrum penicillin. At the Start smart then focus review the team amends to a narrower agent, plans a switch from intravenous to oral treatment once she meets the criteria, and documents a stop date. Pneumonia itself is not on the list of diseases doctors must notify, but the team remembers that invasive pneumococcal infection can be prevented in older adults by vaccination, which is offered at 65.

debrief: Think 'could this be sepsis?' in anyone with signs of infection; temperature may be normal (NICE NG253).
In acute hospitals a NEWS2 of 7 or more means high risk: antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating the score.
Take cultures before the first dose where this does not delay treatment; they make later narrowing possible.
Neutrophilia, raised CRP and raised lactate each map onto the innate response and its dysregulation.
Review at 48–72 hours: cease, amend, refer, extend or switch.

cases.title: A measles case in halls of residence

steps.text: An 18-year-old first-year student who recently returned from visiting relatives abroad has four days of fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes. Today a blotchy red rash began behind her ears and on her face and is spreading downwards. She does not think she had MMR as a child.

ask.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
ask.why: A prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis followed by a blotchy rash starting on the face and behind the ears and spreading downwards, in someone unvaccinated after travel, is classic measles. Chickenpox gives itchy vesicles in crops. Scarlet fever follows a sore throat with a fine, rough rash. Meningococcal septicaemia gives a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash in a rapidly unwell person and should be considered in anyone with fever and a rash, but the prodrome here fits measles.

steps.text: The GP strongly suspects measles and sends samples for confirmation.

ask.q: What should the GP do about notification (checked November 2026)?
options: Notify now on clinical suspicion; measles is urgent, so phone the local health protection team within 24 hours and report online within 3 days
Wait for laboratory confirmation before notifying
Notify only if a second linked case appears
Ask the student's consent and do not notify if she refuses
ask.why: Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 the duty arises on suspicion. Measles is classed as urgent, so UKHSA asks for a phone call to the health protection team within 24 hours as well as the report within 3 days. Waiting for results delays contact tracing; one case is enough; statutory notification does not need consent.

steps.text: The health protection team assesses the halls, where 400 students share kitchens and common rooms. For planning, they take measles R0 as 15 and use an illustrative two-dose vaccine effectiveness of 97%.

ask.q: Using H = 1 − 1/R0, roughly what vaccine coverage is needed to reach the herd immunity threshold?
ask.why: H = 1 − 1/15 ≈ 0.933. Coverage = 0.933 ÷ 0.97 ≈ 0.962, about 96%. About 93% is the threshold itself, ignoring vaccine failure. About 91% multiplies by 0.97 instead of dividing. About 7% is 1/R0, the proportion that can stay susceptible.

steps.text: Two of her flatmates have no record of MMR: one is 16 weeks pregnant, and the other takes strong immunosuppressive drugs after a kidney transplant.

ask.q: Why should these two contacts not simply be given MMR(V) now, and what kind of protection can be considered instead?
options: MMR(V) is an inactivated vaccine that works too slowly, so antibiotics are given instead
MMR(V) is a live vaccine, generally avoided in pregnancy and significant immunosuppression; passive immunity with immunoglobulin can be considered by the health protection team
Contacts never need protection because measles is a mild illness
They should be given a conjugate vaccine, which gives immediate protection
ask.why: Live attenuated vaccines replicate and are generally avoided in pregnancy and significant immunosuppression. Immunoglobulin gives immediate, short-lived passive immunity without needing the contact's own response; UKHSA guidance offers human normal immunoglobulin to susceptible pregnant contacts, ideally within 72 hours of exposure. MMR(V) is live, not inactivated, and antibiotics do not treat viruses. Measles can be severe, especially in pregnancy and immunosuppression. Conjugate vaccines target bacterial polysaccharides, and no vaccine gives immediate protection.

steps.text: Outcome: measles is confirmed. Susceptible contacts are identified; those who can have MMR are offered it to protect against future exposure and close the immunity gap, and the pregnant flatmate is assessed promptly for immunoglobulin. The university runs a catch-up campaign, with drop-in sessions to make vaccination convenient for students who missed doses in childhood.

debrief: Measles is notifiable and urgent: notify on suspicion, by phone to the health protection team within 24 hours.
Very high R0 means a herd immunity threshold above 90%; coverage targets must allow for vaccine failure.
Live vaccines are generally avoided in pregnancy and significant immunosuppression; immunoglobulin gives passive protection.
Outbreak control combines case finding, contact assessment, vaccination and easier access (convenience).

osce.title: Hand hygiene with alcohol handrub
steps: Decide whether alcohol handrub is appropriate: use soap and water instead if hands are visibly soiled, or if the patient has vomiting, diarrhoea or suspected C. difficile or norovirus
Follow local dress policy (commonly bare below the elbows): remove watch and jewellery, roll up sleeves and cover cuts with a waterproof dressing
Apply a palmful of handrub into a cupped hand, enough to cover all surfaces
Right palm over the back of the left hand with fingers interlaced, then swap hands
Palm to palm with fingers interlaced
Backs of the fingers against the opposite palm with fingers interlocked
Rotational rubbing of each thumb clasped in the opposite palm
Rotational rubbing, backwards and forwards, with clasped fingertips in the opposite palm, both hands
Keep rubbing until hands are dry (about 20–30 seconds in all); do not wipe the rub off

State when hand hygiene is needed: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings
tips: Thumbs and fingertips are easy to miss, so make each step deliberate.
Gloves do not replace hand hygiene: clean hands before putting gloves on and after taking them off.
Say out loud why you chose rub or soap and water; examiners look for the C. difficile and norovirus exception.

interpret.title: Fever and productive cough
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 45-year-old man has had three days of fever and cough with green sputum. Which interpretation fits these results best? (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Lymphocytosis, typical of a viral infection
Neutrophilia with a high CRP, typical of an acute bacterial infection such as pneumonia
interpret.why: Neutrophils are 15.9 ×10⁹/L (about twice the upper limit) and account for most of the raised white count, with a markedly raised CRP: the classic picture of acute bacterial infection. Neutrophils are recruited in large numbers to bacterial infection, and IL-6 drives the liver to make CRP.
optWhy: Lymphocytes are 1.3 ×10⁹/L, within the typical range, so there is no lymphocytosis.
Eosinophils are 0.2 ×10⁹/L, within range.
Neutrophils are raised, not low.
Correct: neutrophils drive the raised white count and CRP is high.

interpret.title: Sore throat and tiredness in a student
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 19-year-old has had a sore throat, fever, enlarged neck lymph nodes and marked tiredness for ten days. Which interpretation fits these results best? (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Lymphocytosis with reactive lymphocytes, typical of a viral infection such as glandular fever (Epstein–Barr virus)
interpret.why: The raised white count is driven by lymphocytes (9.1 ×10⁹/L), and the film shows reactive lymphocytes, with only a modest CRP rise. In glandular fever, Epstein–Barr virus infects B cells and large numbers of activated T cells (mainly CD8) expand in response; these appear on the film as reactive (atypical) lymphocytes, an adaptive response to an intracellular pathogen.
optWhy: Neutrophils are 3.4 ×10⁹/L, within range, so there is no neutrophilia.
Eosinophils are 0.1 ×10⁹/L, within range.
Correct: lymphocytes are raised with reactive forms on the film, the expected adaptive response to a virus.
Lymphocytes are raised, not low.

interpret.title: Returned traveller with itch and cough
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 30-year-old returned from several months working in rural sub-Saharan Africa has an itchy rash and a dry cough. Which interpretation fits these results best? (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Normal results, because the total white count is within range
Eosinophilia, pointing towards a helminth (worm) infection driven by a Th2 response
Lymphocytosis, typical of a viral infection
interpret.why: Eosinophils are 2.4 ×10⁹/L, about six times the typical upper limit, even though the total white count is normal. Helminths are too large to engulf; they drive a Th2 response (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) with IgE and eosinophils, so eosinophilia in a returned traveller is a strong clue to a worm infection.
optWhy: A normal total count can hide an abnormal differential; always read each cell type.
Correct: eosinophils are markedly raised, the classic clue to helminth infection.
Neutrophils are 5.1 ×10⁹/L, within range.
Lymphocytes are 2.2 ×10⁹/L, within range.

interpret.title: Fever after chemotherapy
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 58-year-old woman had chemotherapy for breast cancer 10 days ago and now has a temperature of 38.4 °C and feels shivery. Which interpretation is most important? (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Severe neutropenia: she is at high risk of rapidly progressive bacterial and fungal infection, so suspected neutropenic sepsis needs immediate assessment
Expected after chemotherapy, so a routine review in a few days is enough
interpret.why: Her neutrophil count is 0.2 ×10⁹/L, a tenth of the lower limit. Without neutrophils, bacteria and fungi can spread rapidly and the usual signs of inflammation (such as pus) may be muted. NICE NG253 says to suspect neutropenic sepsis in people with possible infection who are having or have had systemic anticancer treatment within the last 30 days (checked October 2026), and suspected neutropenic sepsis is treated as a medical emergency.
optWhy: Correct: profound neutropenia with fever after chemotherapy is an emergency.
Low counts are expected after chemotherapy, but fever with neutropenia is still an emergency, not a routine finding.
Lymphocytes are low (0.6 ×10⁹/L), not raised.
Eosinophils are not reported in these results and nothing points to a helminth; the dangerous finding is the very low neutrophil count.

interpret.title: Hepatitis B check for a medical student
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A medical student who completed a hepatitis B vaccine course last year has these results. Which interpretation fits best? (Expected results shown are typical; laboratories differ.)
options: Immune because of past natural infection
interpret.why: The vaccine contains hepatitis B surface antigen only, so it produces antibody to surface antigen (anti-HBs) but not to core antigen. Anti-HBs alone, with no HBsAg and no anti-HBc, therefore indicates immunity from vaccination.
optWhy: Correct: anti-HBs alone is the vaccine-induced pattern.
Natural infection would also produce anti-HBc, which is not detected.
Current infection would show HBsAg (with anti-HBc); HBsAg is not detected.
Anti-HBs is detected, so she has responded and is immune.

interpret.title: Weight loss and oral thrush
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 41-year-old man with weight loss and oral thrush is newly diagnosed with HIV. Which interpretation fits best? (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: A normal CD4 count, so the thrush is unrelated to HIV
Lymphocytosis typical of an acute viral infection
Advanced immunosuppression (CD4 below 200 per microlitre): high risk of opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia
An undetectable viral load, so there is no risk of transmission
interpret.why: HIV destroys CD4 T cells. A count of 140 cells per microlitre is below 200, the level used in the US CDC surveillance definition of stage 3 HIV (AIDS), and T-cell loss explains opportunistic infections such as oral candidiasis and Pneumocystis pneumonia. Effective treatment would suppress the viral load and let the CD4 count recover.
optWhy: 140 per microlitre is far below the typical range.
Lymphocytes are 0.8 ×10⁹/L, below range, not raised.
Correct: a CD4 count of 140 per microlitre indicates advanced immunosuppression.
The viral load is 85,000 copies/mL, clearly detectable; U=U applies only once the virus is suppressed on treatment.
